passages.title: Oath by the star: revelation, not whim
passages.tafsir:
Allah opens this surah by swearing an oath — and the thing He swears to defend is the character and the speech of His Messenger ﷺ. Ayah 1 is the oath; ayat 2–4 are what the oath is sworn about: this man you know so well has not lost his way, and the words coming from his mouth are not his own invention but revelation. The four ayat hold together as one argument: a witness is called (the star), a verdict is delivered (he is neither astray nor deviant), and the source of his speech is named (wahy — revelation).

## The gathering that ended in prostration

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Sūrah an-Najm was the first chapter the Prophet ﷺ proclaimed in Makkah — this is transmitted from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, as cited in Qurtubi — and that it is the first sūrah in which a verse of *sajdah* (prostration) was revealed.

Al-Bukhari recorded that ʿAbdullāh [ibn Masʿūd] said: "Sūrat an-Najm was the first Sūrah in which a prostration was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ (recited it in Makkah) and prostrated. Those who were with him did the same, except an old man who took a handful of soil and prostrated on it. Later on, I saw him killed as a disbeliever; he was Umayyah bin Khalaf." Ibn Kathir adds that al-Bukhari placed this hadith in several places of his Sahih, and that Muslim, Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i also recorded it through various chains from Abu Ishaq from ʿAbdullāh.

Sit with the scene. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as a strange thing that happened on that occasion: the Prophet ﷺ finished reciting the sūrah before a mixed gathering of Muslims and disbelievers, and prostrated along with his followers — and the disbelievers prostrated too, all but one proud and arrogant man who took a handful of soil, applied it to his forehead and said, "this is enough." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there is a difference of opinion over that man's name; Ibn Kathir's narration names him as Umayyah bin Khalaf.) ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, who transmitted the report, later saw that same man lying dead in a state of disbelief.

That handful of soil is the whole tragedy of arrogance in one gesture. The truth was strong enough to bend the rest of the gathering to the ground; his pride was strong enough to invent a substitute for surrender. He went through a motion that resembled prostration while withholding the one thing prostration is — submission.

## Ayah 1: why swear by a star, and by a falling one?

**The word najm.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *najm* means a star; as a common noun any star is a *najm*, and its plural is *nujūm*. But on some occasions *najm* refers specifically to *Thurayyā* — the Pleiades, a loose cluster of many hundreds of stars, six of which are visible to ordinary sight. Some scholars, taking the word as a proper noun, read it here that way. Ibn Kathir preserves that reading from Mujahid, reported by Ibn Abi Najih: "The star refers to Pleiades when it sets at Fajr." Farrāʼ and Hasan Basri, as Qurtubi relates, prefer the first interpretation — the common noun, any star — and that is the reading behind the translation "By the stars when they fade away."

**The word hawā.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verb *hawā* means to fall or plunge, and that when stars fall, they set — sinking below the horizon. A second early reading is recorded by Ibn Kathir from ad-Dahhak, who said of the star's falling: "When the Shayatin are shot with it" — that is, the devils.

**Why an oath at all, and is it permitted?** Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Abi Hatim's report from ash-Shaʿbi and others: the Creator swears by whatever He wills among His creation, but the created only vow by the Creator. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same principle — that the Creator, for various wise reasons, swears by whatever He wills among His creation, while His created beings may swear only by the Creator and are not allowed to swear by anything else — noting that this is explained in detail in Sūrah as-Sāffāt. It is a rule worth holding on to: Allah may swear by whichever of His creatures He wills; a human being may swear only by Allah.

**The fittingness of this particular oath.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a beautiful reason for choosing the star here: the Arabs were used to determining their course and direction by the movements of the stars, and were guided in their travels by them across the sandy waste of Arabia. Probably, then, the underlying wisdom is that as they are guided in their journeys by the stars, so they would now be led to the goal and end of their spiritual journey by the star par excellence — the Prophet ﷺ himself. The oath is not decoration; it is the argument in miniature. You already trust a star to tell you where you are. Here is the one you should trust with where you are going.

Ibn Kathir also sets this oath beside another: "So, I swear by the setting of the stars. And verily, that is indeed a great oath, if you but know. That is indeed an honorable recitation. In a Book well-guarded. Which none can touch but the pure. A revelation from the Lord of all that exists." (56:75–80) The pattern is identical — stars sworn by, and revelation as the thing established.

## Ayah 2: the verdict of the oath

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the grammar plainly: ayah 1 is the *qasam* (the oath) and ayah 2 is the *jawāb al-qasam* — the statement the oath is sworn to establish. Ibn Kathir says the same: this contains the subject of the oath, the witness that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is sane and a follower of truth.

**Two different failures, both denied.** Ibn Kathir draws the line sharply:

- Going astray is the failure of the ignorant — the one who does not proceed on any path with knowledge. He is lost because he never had the map.
- Erring is the failure of the knowledgeable — the one who knows the truth yet deviates from it intentionally to something else. He is lost because he had the map and chose otherwise.

Between them they exhaust the ways a guide can fail you: he can be sincere but wrong, or informed but crooked. Ayah 2 denies both. Ibn Kathir concludes that Allah thereby exonerated His Messenger ﷺ and his message from being similar to the misguided ways of the Christians and the erroneous paths of the Jews — such as knowing the truth and hiding it while abiding by falsehood. Rather, he ﷺ and the glorious message Allah sent him with are on the perfect straight path, following guidance and what is correct. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the positive side of it: the path towards which he ﷺ is calling people is the perfectly straight path, leading to the desired goal of Allah's good pleasure; he is following the right guidance and has not deviated from the path of righteousness.

**"Your companion" — sāhibukum.** Here is one of the most piercing word-choices in the passage, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out. On this occasion the Qur'an does not refer to him ﷺ by his blessed name, nor as a Messenger, nor as a Prophet. It says *your companion*. There is a subtle rebuke to the pagans of Makkah in it: this man is not an outsider, nor a stranger to them. He was their constant companion — born among them, spending his childhood among them, growing up as a youth among them, living a whole lifetime among them — and all that time they looked upon him as a paragon of honesty, integrity and truthfulness, calling him *al-Amīn*, the Honest One.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then presses the question they could not answer: now, after his claim to prophethood, they dare impute to him a sin as heinous as forging lies against Allah? A man who withheld himself from telling lies about men — how could he possibly forge lies against Allah? How inconsistent is their attitude?

That word also disarms the excuse of distance. The evidence was not in a far country or an old book; it was the neighbour whose word they had trusted their whole lives.

## Ayat 3–4: he does not speak from whim

Ibn Kathir explains ayah 3 as asserting that nothing the Prophet ﷺ utters is of his own desire or wish, and ayah 4 as meaning that he only conveys to the people what he was commanded to convey — in its entirety, without additions or deletions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the conclusion bluntly: it is absolutely impossible for the Messenger ﷺ to forge lies and impute them to Allah.

Note the two halves. "Without additions" — he does not embroider what he was given, does not soften it for a hostile audience or sharpen it to win an argument. "Without deletions" — he does not hold back the part that costs him. Both are failures of a messenger who serves his own *hawā* (desire, whim — the very word ayah 3 uses); ayah 3 rules both out.

### From the Sunnah: two narrations Ibn Kathir brings here

**"I said what I said."** Imam Ahmad recorded that Abu Umamah heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that numbers similar to the two tribes, or one of them — Rabiʿah and Mudar — will enter Paradise on account of the intercession of one man who is not a Prophet. A man asked, "O Allah's Messenger! Is not Rabiʿah a subtribe of Mudar?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, "I said what I said."

He does not revise under questioning, and he does not fill the gap with his own reasoning. What was given is what is delivered — exactly. That short answer is ayah 3 in action.

**"Write!"** Imam Ahmad recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr said: "I used to record everything I heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ so it would be preserved. The Quraysh discouraged me from this, saying, 'You record everything you hear from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, even though he is human and sometimes speaks when he is angry?' I stopped recording the Hadiths for a while, but later mentioned what they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said, 'Write! By He in Whose Hand is my soul, every word that comes out of me is the Truth.'" Ibn Kathir notes that Abu Dawud also collected this hadith.

The objection raised to ʿAbdullāh is exactly the doubt these ayat answer — *he is only human, and human speech carries mood.* The reply is a permission and a guarantee at once: write it down, because what comes out of me is truth.

### What kind of revelation? The two types

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a real question here, and answers it with care. If everything he ﷺ says is revelation, what about the authentic reports in which he promulgated one ruling and revelation later descended and changed it — which suggests the earlier ruling was based on his own reasoning rather than Allah's law?

From an analysis of the various traditions in Bukhari, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes categories of *wahy* (inspiration or revelation):

1. **Wording and meaning both directly from Allah.** This is the Qur'an.
2. **Meaning from Allah, expressed by the Messenger ﷺ in his own words.** This is Hadith or Sunnah.

Within the second type, the content sometimes lays down injunctions or rules of conduct in clear and express terms; at other times it establishes a general principle from which the Messenger ﷺ derives laws on the basis of *ijtihād* (disciplined reasoning) or analogy, and promulgates them. In that derivation, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān acknowledges, there does exist the possibility of a mistake of judgment.

But — and this is the characteristic of the Messenger ﷺ and the other Prophets, upon them be peace — if they commit any error of judgment, Allah sends down a revelation to amend it, so that they do not unwittingly persist in a mistaken ijtihād. Unlike other scholars of ijtihād, who can persist in their erroneous conclusions; yet even their error is not only forgiven — they also receive one reward for exerting their utmost effort in comprehending the rule of religion to the fullest extent, as authentic and well-known traditions bear testimony.

So the objection dissolves. Because the general principle itself descended from Allah, all the laws derived from it are said to be revelation from Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the discussion with the scholar's own humility: *Allah knows best!*

## Living it

**Trust the guide the way you trust the star.** The oath in ayah 1 was chosen for people who staked their lives on reading the sky. The application is the same for us: the Prophet ﷺ is the fixed point you navigate by, not one voice among the many competing for your attention.

**Take the Sunnah with the weight ayah 4 gives it.** If nothing he ﷺ conveyed came from his own whim, then his teaching is not optional colour around the Qur'an. "Write!" was said for a reason.

**Beware the handful of soil.** The man in Ibn Masʿūd's report did not deny what he heard; he simply refused to put his forehead where everyone else put theirs, and invented a gesture that let him keep his pride. Half-surrender that protects the ego is the counterfeit these ayat expose.

**Watch your own desires.** The two failures denied of the Prophet ﷺ in ayah 2 are precisely the two we are prone to: speaking about the religion without knowledge, and knowing the truth but bending it because desire pulls the other way. The cure for both is what the passage itself models — speak from what was revealed, not from what you wish were true.

passages.title: The mighty one and the first vision
passages.tafsir:
**What holds these ayat together.** Ayah 4 has just declared that what the Prophet ﷺ speaks is nothing but revelation revealed to him. Ayat 5–12 answer the question that immediately follows: *revealed how, and through whom?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that from ayah 5 onward the subject-matter is revelation from Allah — that the Qur'an is a record of verbal revelation given to the Prophet ﷺ, sent down in such a way that no possibility of confusion or error ever existed.

## The chain of transmission

The scholars of hadith, to verify that a report really comes from the Prophet ﷺ, trace the full chain of authorities back to him. In these ayat, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, Allah sets out the chain for the Qur'an itself: Allah is the ultimate Source from whom the revelation originates, and Jibrīl (peace be upon him) is the transmitting authority between Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. The ayat then describe Jibrīl as magnificent in status and mighty in power — which, says Maʿārif, confirms his honesty and integrity as the transmitting authority, exactly as a hadith scholar establishes the integrity of a narrator. The passage is, in effect, the Qur'an's own *isnād* (chain of transmission).

Maʿārif's teacher Maulana Sayyid Muhammad Anwar Shah Kashmiri set out the structure this way: ayah 4 is the preamble announcing revelation; ayat 5–9 describe the qualities of the medium through whom it comes; ayah 10 is the complement that returns to the Sender.

## Who is "one of mighty power"?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays both readings out.

**The first reading** takes these ayat to relate to the Miʿrāj (the Ascension), so that the qualities and acts described are all of Allah — that Allah taught His Prophet ﷺ directly without any intermediary. Among the Companions, Anas and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them) are reported to have adopted this, and *Tafsīr Mazharī* gave it preference.

**The second reading** — that of many Companions, of the *tābiʿīn* (the Companions' pupils), and of other leading commentators — is that "one of mighty power" and the qualities and acts described in these ayat belong to the angel Jibrīl (peace be upon him), and that what the Prophet ﷺ saw was Jibrīl in the original shape in which Allah created him. Maʿārif gives the supporting arguments:

- Sūrah an-Najm is one of the very early sūrahs; according to ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him) it is the first sūrah the Prophet ﷺ recited in public in Makkah, whereas the Miʿrāj took place much later. (Maʿārif concedes this argument may be debatable.)
- The stronger proof: in a tradition recorded in the *Musnad* of Aḥmad, the Prophet ﷺ himself interprets these ayat as relating to seeing Jibrīl.

The decisive testimony is ʿĀʾishah's. Masrūq asked her about "And indeed he saw him in the clear horizon" (81:23) and "And indeed he saw him at a second descent" (53:13). She replied, "I was the first among this Ummah to ask Allah's Messenger ﷺ about it," and he said, *"That was Jibrīl"* — and he saw him only twice in his actual and real figure; he saw Jibrīl descend from heaven to earth, so huge that he covered the whole horizon between the sky and the earth. Ibn Kathīr notes that this hadith is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs through ash-Shaʿbī, and Maʿārif adds that the wording in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim is almost the same.

Ibn Kathīr quotes all these narrations and concludes that the perception and the proximity in these ayat refer to seeing and being close to Jibrīl. Maʿārif reports that among the Companions this is the view of ʿĀʾishah, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī and Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with them), and that Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Imām Rāzī, Nawawī in his commentary on Muslim, Ibn Ḥajar in *Fatḥ ul-Bārī*, and Maʿārif's own mentor Maulana Ashraf ʿAlī normally preferred this reading too.

On this reading, ayat 5–12 describe the *first* of the two sightings; the second, on the night of the Miʿrāj, is mentioned later in the sūrah, at ayah 13.

## The words themselves

**"Mighty in power" (ayah 5)** — *shadīd al-quwā*. Ibn Kathīr states that the Message the Prophet ﷺ brought to people was taught to him by one mighty in power, and that this is Jibrīl (peace be upon him). He links the description to Allah's words elsewhere: "Verily, this is the Word of a most honourable messenger, owner of power, with the Lord of the Throne, obeyed and trustworthy" (81:19–21).

**"Dhū mirrah" (ayah 6)** — Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd explained *Dhū Mirrah* as mighty in power. Ibn Kathīr notes that it is the same word used in an authentic hadith reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayrah, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that charity is not allowed for a rich person, nor for a *dhū mirrah sawiyy* — a strong person of sound mind and body. Maʿārif draws out why this matters: *mirrah* means strength or vigour, and this is another quality of Jibrīl, that he is no weakling, so that it may not be suspected that a devil could intercept the angel carrying the revelation and snatch it away.

**"Then he rose" — *fastawā* (ayah 6)** — Ibn Kathīr reports from al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatādah and ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas that this refers to the angel Jibrīl. Maʿārif explains *istawā* as to be or become straight, to level: when the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibrīl the first time, the angel was descending from the heaven, and settled straight upon the highest part of the horizon.

**"On the highest horizon" (ayah 7)** — Ibn Kathīr: Jibrīl rose to the highest part of the horizon. ʿIkrimah said, "The highest horizon, where the morning comes from"; Mujāhid said, "It is the place of sunrise." Maʿārif adds why the *highest* horizon: the lower part of the horizon, which seems to be adjacent to the earth, is normally hidden from sight — so the angel was shown on the uppermost horizon, where he could be seen clearly.

**"Then he drew near and came down" (ayah 8)** — Maʿārif: *danā* means to draw near and *tadallā* means to hang or to come down. Jibrīl drew near by coming down.

**"Two bows' length or less" (ayah 9)** — *qāba qawsayn*. Ibn Kathīr explains that Jibrīl came closer to Muhammad ﷺ as he was descending to him on earth, and that the distance between them became two bow lengths with the bows extended to full length, according to Mujāhid and Qatādah. Maʿārif takes *qāb* as the distance between the curved handle of a bow and the taut chord that releases arrows — about the length of one hand — and then unlocks the image with an ancient Arab custom: when two people pledged themselves to firm friendship, each would turn the wooden part of his bow towards himself and the chord towards the other, and when the chords were joined this was regarded as a proclamation of proximity, love and affection. Read that way, ayah 9 is not merely a measurement; it is the old sign of a bond sealed.

**"Or less" (ayah 9)** — Ibn Kathīr treats this as a Qur'anic idiom that removes doubt rather than creating it. Compare "your hearts were hardened and became as stones or even worse in hardness" (2:74); "And We sent him to a hundred thousand people or even more" (37:147). In each case the sense is *at least that, and more* — not less; and so, says Ibn Kathīr, this verifies the facts mentioned, leaving no doubt or means of refutation. Maʿārif states: such intimacy with Jibrīl is mentioned to confirm that the revelation he delivered is truly from Allah and was heard with absolute accuracy in every detail, and to allay the suspicion that the Prophet ﷺ might not have recognised Jibrīl.

## The first sighting, and what came before it

Ibn Kathīr's account, as Maʿārif relays it: the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibrīl in his original shape for the first time at the very beginning of prophethood, when Jibrīl descended with the very first instalment of revelation and delivered to him Sūrah *Iqraʾ*. After that came the interval — a pause in revelation that caused terrible grief. Time and again the thought crossed his mind that he should go to the top of a mountain. Whenever such a situation arose, Jibrīl would call out to him invisibly from the air: *"O Muhammad! You are Allah's Messenger; you are true; and I am Jibrīl."*

Then one day Jibrīl was in an open field at Baṭḥāʾ in his original shape, with six hundred wings that had covered the entire horizon; he came close to Allah's Messenger ﷺ and delivered the revelation to him. On that occasion, says Ibn Kathīr, the reality of Jibrīl's greatness and his majestic value in the sight of Allah became manifest to Allah's Messenger ﷺ. Maʿārif adds that some of the versions narrate that when he saw Jibrīl in his actual shape the first time, the Prophet ﷺ became unconscious, and Jibrīl then came very close to him in the shape of a human being.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw Jibrīl in his original shape having six hundred wings, each wing filling the side of the horizon, with a colourful array, and pearls and rubies falling from each wing as much as only Allah knows; Ibn Kathīr notes that only Imām Aḥmad collected this hadith.

Imām Aḥmad also recorded from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ asked Jibrīl to appear to him in his original shape, and Jibrīl said, "Invoke your Lord." The Prophet ﷺ invoked his Lord, and a great huge figure appeared to him from the east and kept rising and spreading; when he saw Jibrīl in his original shape he was knocked unconscious, and Jibrīl came down, revived him, and wiped the saliva from his cheeks. Ibn Kathīr notes that only Aḥmad collected this hadith.

## "Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed" (ayah 10)

Ibn Kathīr allows two readings and says both are correct: that Jibrīl conveyed to Allah's servant Muhammad ﷺ whatever he conveyed; or that Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad ﷺ whatever He revealed, through Jibrīl. Maʿārif takes the pronouns to refer to Allah — Allah revealed to His servant Muhammad ﷺ through the medium of Jibrīl, whom He had attached so intimately to him.

Maʿārif raises the objection itself, calling it academic rather than real: if the pronouns throughout these ayat refer to Jibrīl, does referring the pronouns of ayah 10 to Allah not produce *intishār ud-ḍamāʾir*, an inconsistency of pronouns? The answer, from Maulana Anwar Shah Kashmiri, is that there is neither contextual confusion nor pronominal ambiguity: ayah 4 already said "It is nothing but revelation revealed," and obviously the One who sends down revelation is Allah and none else.

**"What He revealed"** is left deliberately unspecified. Maʿārif notes that *mā* ("whatever") is sometimes used to denote honour, surprise, magnificence, grandeur or emphasis — here, to indicate the majestic status of the revelation. As to its content, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said Allah revealed to him, "Did He not find you an orphan?" (93:6) and "And have We not raised high your fame?" (94:4). Maʿārif, citing a hadith recorded in chapter one of the Ṣaḥīḥ of Bukhārī, holds that the revelation sent down at this time was the initial verses of Sūrah al-Muddaththir — and closes, as one should, with "Allah knows best."

Not "His Prophet," but **"His servant."** At the height of the encounter, he is named by his servanthood.

## "The heart did not lie about what it saw" (ayah 11)

*Fuʾād* means heart. Maʿārif explains: whatever the eyes saw, the heart did not err in grasping it. That erring is described in the ayah as *kidhb*, lying.

Maʿārif adds that Ibn Jarīr, with his own chain of transmitters, reports that ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, interpreting this ayah, said that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibrīl clad in a green garment filling the entire space between heaven and earth.

Maʿārif then observes that the Arabic verb *raʾā* originally means to see with the physical eyes, after which the heart grasps and comprehends what was seen — which means, says Maʿārif, that there is no need to take *ruʾyah* here in the figurative sense of "seeing with the heart," as al-Qurṭubī did.

Maʿārif anticipates a philosophical objection — that *idrāk*, perception and comprehension, belongs to the intellect rather than the heart — and answers from the Qur'an itself, where *qalb* (heart) stands for *ʿaql* (intellect): "they have hearts with which they do not comprehend" (7:179).

## Did the Prophet ﷺ see his Lord?

The early authorities differed.

**Reported from Ibn ʿAbbās**, in a narration Muslim records, on ayah 11 together with 53:13: "He saw Allah twice in his heart." Ibn Kathīr notes that Simāk reported similarly from ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, and that Abū Ṣāliḥ, as-Suddī and several others said the same.

**ʿĀʾishah rejected the idea of a seeing with the eyes vehemently.** Imām Aḥmad recorded that Masrūq asked her, "O Mother of the faithful, has Muhammad ﷺ seen his Lord?" She said, "Glorious is Allah! My hair is standing on end because of what you said." Whoever tells you that Muhammad ﷺ has seen his Lord has lied — and she recited "No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision" (6:103) and "It is not given to any human being that Allah should speak to him unless it be by revelation, or from behind a veil" (42:51). Whoever tells you that Muhammad ﷺ knew what the morrow will bring has uttered a lie — and she recited "Verily, Allah, with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, He sends down the rain, and knows that which is in the wombs" (31:34). And whoever tells you that Muhammad ﷺ has hidden any part of the Message has lied — and she recited "O Messenger, proclaim what has been sent down to you from your Lord" (5:67). She went on: "However, he saw Jibrīl twice in his original shape."

**Muslim records** that Abū Dharr said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Have you seen your Lord?' He said, *'How can I see Him, since there was a light?'*" In another narration, *"I only saw a light."*

Ibn Kathīr then reports that, relying on "Indeed he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord" (53:18) together with "in order that We might show him of Our signs" (17:1), **some scholars of Ahl us-Sunnah said that the Prophet ﷺ did not see Allah during the Isrāʾ journey**, reasoning that had he seen his Lord, Allah would have conveyed this news and the Prophet ﷺ would have narrated it to the people.

## "Will you then dispute with him about what he saw?" (ayah 12)

Ibn Kathīr reads ayah 11 and ayah 12 together — "The heart lied not in what he saw. Will you then dispute with him about what he saw?"

## What this asks of us

**Certainty about the Qur'an.** Maʿārif's point is the passage's point: a secured chain from the Source, through a transmitter whose strength and integrity are certified, to a receiver whose eye and heart both held true. When you open the muṣḥaf, you stand at the end of that chain.

**Awe before the unseen.** A single created servant of Allah, appearing in his original shape, covered the entire horizon — and in the narration Imām Aḥmad records from Ibn ʿAbbās, the sight of him left the Prophet ﷺ unconscious. If that is the messenger, what of the One who sends him?

**Patience in the interval.** Allah did not abandon him in the interval; the comfort came even while the comforter stayed unseen, and the waiting ended in the sight of Jibrīl in his original shape.

passages.title: The second vision at the Lote Tree
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat carry the Prophet ﷺ to the furthest point any creature travels. Having insisted in ayat 11–12 that his heart did not lie about what his eyes took in, Allah now names the second occasion of that seeing: not on the horizon above Makkah, but in the highest heaven, at the Lote Tree of the Ultimate Boundary, with the Garden of Abode beside it, the tree drowned in a covering splendour — and a witness whose gaze never once slipped. A single event, the Night of Miʿrāj, described from four angles: **when** (ayah 13), **where** (ayat 14–15), **what it looked like** (ayah 16), and **how he received it** (ayat 17–18).

## "A second descent" — locating the moment

The Arabic in ayah 13 is *nazlatan ukhrā*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders as "another time or at another descent". It notes that, according to the overwhelming majority, this *nuzūl* is the second descent of Jibrīl (peace be upon him). So the sūrah is describing two distinct sightings of the angel in the form Allah originally created him in.

Where was the first? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pins it down using a narration of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Bukhārī, in the chapter entitled "How the revelation started". Speaking of the temporary break in revelation, the Prophet ﷺ said that while he was walking he heard a voice from the sky, raised his eyes, and saw the Angel who had come to him at Ḥirāʼ seated on a chair between heaven and earth. He was struck with awe, returned home and said, "Wrap me up, wrap me up" — and Allah sent down *Yā ayyuhal-muddaththir* (74:1–5). "Then revelation became copious and came in succession."

So the first vision was on this earth, in Makkah, at the uppermost horizon, before the Night Journey. The second, ayah 14 tells us, was at Sidrat al-Muntahā in the seventh heaven, which places it on the Night of Miʿrāj. Two sightings, two worlds, one angel: the Makkans were being told that the man delivering this Qurʼān had met its carrier face to face, twice, in two entirely different orders of reality.

## Whom did he see? An honest account of a real disagreement

Both Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treat this openly as a matter the scholars differed over.

**The view that it was Jibrīl.** ʿĀʼishah (may Allah be pleased with her) held this with force. Masrūq reports asking her whether Muḥammad ﷺ saw his Lord; she said his question made her hair stand on end. She recited "No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision" (6:103) and "It is not given to any human being that Allah should speak to him unless by revelation, or from behind a veil" (42:51), and named three things a person lies about if he claims them: that the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, that he knew what the morrow will bring (reciting 31:34), and that he concealed any part of the Message (reciting 5:67). "However," she said, "he saw Jibrīl twice in his original shape." In a further narration recorded by Imam Aḥmad, Masrūq put ayah 13 and 81:23 to her directly, and she answered: "I was the first among this Ummah to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it." He ﷺ said, **"That was Jibrīl."** She added that he saw him only twice in his actual and real figure, descending from heaven to earth, so huge that he covered the whole horizon between the sky and the earth. Ibn Kathīr notes this ḥadīth is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs by way of Ash-Shaʿbī. Ibn Kathīr himself states that ayah 13 refers to the second time the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw Jibrīl in the shape Allah created him, during the Night of Isrāʼ.

**The view that a vision of Allah is intended.** Muslim records from Ibn ʿAbbās, on ayah 11 and ayah 13, "He saw Allah twice **in his heart**." Ibn Kathīr says the like is reported from ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, As-Suddī and several others — all specifying the heart. Muslim also records that Abū Dharr asked, "Have you seen your Lord?" and the Prophet ﷺ replied, **"How can I see Him since there was a light?"** — in another wording, **"I only saw a light."**

**Where Ibn Kathīr lands.** He reports that some scholars of Ahl us-Sunnah argued from ayah 18 itself that the Prophet ﷺ did not see Allah during the Isrāʼ journey: Allah says he saw *of the greatest signs of his Lord*, not that he saw his Lord — and had he seen Him, Allah would have conveyed that news and the Prophet ﷺ would have narrated it to the people.

**Where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lands.** It notes that the pronoun in ayah 13 admits both readings; that the reference to Jibrīl is perfectly obvious to any scholar, while a hint at the vision of Allah is possible, because seeing requires proximity and closeness and "at the Lote Tree of the Ultimate Boundary" indicates exactly that closeness. It records the settled position that the vision of Allah is not impossible in itself — all the Companions, their immediate followers and the overwhelming majority of the Ummah concur that the people of Paradise and the believers in general will see Him — but that in this mundane world the capacity of human sight is not powerful enough to bear it. Imam Mālik said no human can see Allah in this world because his sight is perishable and Allah is Eternal; in the Hereafter man will be given non-perishable sight, and then nothing will prevent it. Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ said something similar. A narration recorded in Muslim is quoted to make the point explicit: "And know that you shall never see your Lord, until you die." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds that on the Night of Ascension the Prophet ﷺ was called out of this mundane world in the most distinguishable manner, to see the heavens, Paradise and Hell and other great signs — so a vision there would stand as an exception to the general rule. On that basis, the *possibility* of the vision of Allah is confirmed.

Then comes the decisive point. *Possible* is not the same as *happened*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*, under the tafsīr of Sūrah an-Najm, cited the differences of the Companions and their followers, and that Qurṭubī in his *Mufhim* preferred **silence** — declining to decide either way, because this question does not concern our practical life but our belief system, where incontestable evidence is required. In any matter that cannot be proved incontestably, the rule is to observe silence. Its author adopts this as the most sound and circumspect approach, closing with *Allah, the Pure and the Exalted, knows best*. Ibn Kathīr likewise records that Ibn ʿAbbās affirmed that the Prophet ﷺ saw Allah and that a group of righteous predecessors followed him, while other groups of Companions and their followers differed, and he sets out the evidences of both groups.

**A reconciliation.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits an analysis by Maulānā Sayyid Muḥammad Anwar Shāh Kashmīrī, written at the request of Shaykh al-Islām Shabbīr Aḥmad ʿUthmānī for his *Fatḥ al-Mulhim*, the commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim: the opening ten ayat describe Jibrīl, because their expressions — "one of strong faculties", "one of vigour", "then he drew near", "at a distance of two bows' length or even nearer" — apply to the angel directly and candidly, and can be applied to Allah only through laboured interpretation. But from ayah 11 to ayah 18 the subject is Isrāʼ and Miʿrāj, and although the sighting of Jibrīl is mentioned there, it is one part among *many* great signs — and the possibility that "the greatest signs" include the vision of Allah cannot be ruled out. He notes a detail of wording in ayah 12: Allah does not say *qad raʼā*, in the past tense, but *ʿalā mā yarā*, which the commentary renders as "what he will see" — so the Makkans are being told not to dispute what he has seen **or what he will yet see**.

Two things to carry away: the disagreement is real and old, and it runs among the Companions, their followers and the leading authorities themselves, not between orthodoxy and error; and where the arguments do not settle, the tafsīr we are reading declines to declare a winner, and says so.

## The tree at the edge of everything

The word *sidrah* literally denotes the lote tree, and *muntahā* means the place of *intihāʼ*, the end. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān therefore defines Sidrat al-Muntahā as the Lote Tree on the seventh heaven under the Throne of Allah. It notes a narration in Muslim placing the tree on the sixth heaven, and Qurṭubī's reconciliation of the two apparently conflicting versions: its root is on the sixth heaven and its branches spread on the seventh.

Why "the end"? Because the access of the angels generally ends at this point. Ibn Kathīr records from Ibn Masʿūd, through Imam Aḥmad, that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken on the Isrāʼ journey he ascended to Sidrat al-Muntahā in the seventh heaven — "there everything terminates that ascends from the earth and is held there, and terminates everything that descends from above and is held there." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, reporting this subject from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd as recorded by Imam Aḥmad in his *Musnad*, that the divine injunctions first descend from the Throne to Sidrat al-Muntahā and are handed over there to the relevant angels, and that the angels going up from the earth with the books of deeds convey them to this point — beyond which there may be some other way for their presentation to Allah.

Picture it as the frontier post of the created order: the place where the traffic of revelation coming down and of deeds going up changes hands. And a man of Makkah was brought to it.

## The Garden that already exists (ayah 15)

*Maʼwā*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means an abode, a place where one resides or reposes comfortably. Paradise is called *maʼwā* because it is man's original abode: it is where Ādam and Ḥawwāʼ were created, from there they were sent down to the earth, and there the people of Paradise will be sent back to reside permanently. The word turns homesickness into geography.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a point of belief from the ayah: that Paradise **exists at the present moment** — the belief of the overwhelming majority of the Ummah, that Paradise and Hell have been created and are already in existence. The ayah points out that the location of Paradise is on the seventh heaven under the Throne; the seventh heaven is as though the floor of Paradise and its roof is the Throne. It adds that the location of Hell is not explicitly stated anywhere in the Qurʼān or the Prophetic Traditions, and closes that discussion with *Allah knows best* — a good model for how to hold what we have not been told.

## "When there covered the Lote Tree that which covered it" (ayah 16)

The ayah refuses to name what did the covering; the subject is left as *mā yaghshā* — "that which covered". This is language deliberately withholding, and the effect is awe: the thing was past describing, so the description is withheld. Ibn Kathīr says that in the ḥadīths about al-Isrāʼ it was mentioned that the angels, Allah's Light, and spectacular colours covered the Sidrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd: "Golden butterflies were at that time falling on Sidrat al-Muntahā from all sides" — and it seemed as if the tree had been specially decorated for that occasion in honour of the most revered guest, the Prophet ﷺ.

And in the same narration of Ibn Masʿūd on this ayah, recorded by Imam Aḥmad and collected by Muslim, comes what the Prophet ﷺ was **given** there: the five prayers; the concluding verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah (2:284–286); and remission of serious sins for those among his Ummah who do not associate anything with Allah. Whatever else is disputed about that night, this is what came home from it — and two thirds of it is in your hands every day.

## The gaze that did not slip (ayah 17)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two verbs precisely. *Zāgha* is derived from *zaygh*, to become crooked or go astray. *Ṭaghā* is derived from *ṭughyān*, to transgress or exceed the limit. Two verbs, because there are two ways human sight can go awry: it can fail to look at the object directly and turn to some other side, missing what it was brought to see; or it can look at the intended object **and** at other objects too, with the risk of losing sight of the main one and causing confusion. "It did not swerve" closes the first door; "nor did it exceed the limit" closes the second. Ibn ʿAbbās said his sight did not turn right or left; Ibn Kathīr glosses "nor did it transgress" as not exceeding what has been ordained for it.

This is the psychological heart of the passage. A human being is standing at the boundary of the created order, the Garden beside him and unnameable splendour pouring over the tree, and his eyes do exactly what they were told and nothing more. Ibn Kathīr calls this a tremendous quality that demonstrates the Prophet's firm obedience to Allah: **he only did what he was commanded, and did not ask beyond what he was given.** Not a glance of curiosity. Not a grasping after the one sight not offered.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this ayah includes both possibilities of what was seen, and that it further proves the vision took place in a state of wakefulness with his physical eyes — it was not a dream. And it observes that the ayah allays a suspicion worth naming: that human sight sometimes errs or slips, especially when something wonderful or unusually marvellous is put before it.

## "Of the greatest signs of his Lord" (ayah 18)

He saw **of** the signs of his Lord — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase "He has indeed seen a part of the biggest signs of your Lord." A part of them; not the Lord Himself. Ibn Kathīr reads it alongside "in order that We might show him of Our signs" (17:1): signs that testify to Allah's might and greatness. As we saw, this very wording is the argument some scholars of Ahl us-Sunnah used to conclude that the vision of Allah did not occur that night, while Anwar Shāh Kashmīrī read the same phrase as broad enough to leave the possibility open. The passage closes on that deliberate note — the greatest of the signs, seen in part, by one man, on one night.

## Living it

**Restraint is the mark of a true servant.** The practical lesson Ibn Kathīr draws from these six ayat is ayah 17: the Prophet ﷺ took what he was given and did not ask beyond it. Faith is not measured by how much of the unseen you can pry open; it is measured by how well you hold what you were handed.

**Silence is a legitimate answer in creed.** Qurṭubī declined to decide whether the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord, because the matter concerns belief rather than practice and incontestable evidence was unavailable — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adopts that position as the most sound and circumspect. Where the evidence genuinely does not settle a matter of belief, "Allah knows best" is not evasion; it is the discipline.

**Keep the gift in view.** From the furthest station any creature has reached, the Prophet ﷺ brought back the five prayers, the concluding verses of al-Baqarah, and remission for those of his Ummah who associate nothing with Allah. The passage's grandeur has a very ordinary door into it, and you walk through it at every prayer.

passages.title: Lat, Uzza and Manat: mere names
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Having just established that what the Prophet ﷺ saw was true and that his revelation is preserved, the Qur'an turns and asks the Makkans to look hard at what they themselves are worshipping. Ayat 19–20 simply name the three most famous idols of Arabia; ayah 21 exposes the strange theology built around them; ayah 22 calls that division unfair; and ayah 23 delivers the verdict that binds the whole unit together — these are not gods at all, only **names** that men invented and then bowed to.

## Where this falls in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: the preceding verses "declared the Glory of Allah, His Majesty and Dignity," and confirmed and verified in the fullest detail the prophethood and messengership of Muhammad ﷺ and the preservation of his revelation. Against that backdrop, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, these verses carry a subtle rebuke to the pagans of Makkah — that without any proof, instead of adoring so Mighty and Powerful a Creator and Lord, they stoop so low as to worship gods made of wood and stone. And more: they allege that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and according to other narratives that these idols themselves are His daughters.

Ibn Kathir frames it the same way: Allah the Exalted rebukes the idolaters for worshipping idols and taking rivals to Him — people who "built houses for their idols to resemble the Ka'bah built by Prophet Ibrahim, Allah's *Khalil*" (His intimate friend). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, reports the same thing: they built houses for their idols to resemble the Ka'bah. So the worship being confronted here was not a bare superstition; it had houses, and those houses were made to look like the House of Ibrahim.

## Three names the Arabs knew by heart

Ibn Kathir notes that there were other idols in the Arabian Peninsula which the Arabs revered "just as they revered the Ka'bah," and that Allah mentioned these three here **because they were more famous than the others**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says the pagans of Arabia had countless idols, but that these three were the most popular and were worshipped by strong and powerful tribes of Arabia.

### Al-Lāt (ayah 19)

Al-Lāt was a white stone with inscriptions on it. There was a house built around it in At-Tā'if, with curtains, servants and a sacred courtyard. The people of At-Tā'if — the tribe of Thaqīf and their allies — worshipped it, and they would boast to the Arabs, except the Quraysh, that they had Al-Lāt. Muhammad ibn Ishāq narrated that Banū Muʿattib were its custodians and its servants.

Two things about the name are worth pausing over.

First, **Ibn Jarīr** said that they derived Al-Lāt's name from Allah's Name and made it feminine — and he immediately adds, *Allah is far removed from what they ascribe to Him*. Shirk here is not an alternative religion invented from nothing; it is Allah's own Name bent out of shape and hung on a stone.

Second, there is a report on how the shrine began. Ibn Jarīr transmits that, according to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Al-Lāt was **a man** who used to mix *sawīq* (a kind of barley mash) with water for the pilgrims during the time of Jāhiliyyah. When he died, they remained next to his grave — and worshipped him. Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said about this ayah: "Al-Lat was a man who used to mix Sawiq for the pilgrims."

Sit with that. The idol that a whole city boasted of began as a generous man serving drinks to pilgrims. Nobody sat down and decided to invent a false god. Devotion to a good man slid into staying by his grave, and staying by his grave into worship — and generations later a tribe is boasting about a stone. That is exactly why ayah 23 says these are names *you and your fathers* named: the fathers began it, the sons inherited it, and no one along the way was ever handed a proof.

### Al-ʿUzzā (ayah 19)

Ibn Jarīr said they also derived the name of their idol Al-ʿUzzā from Allah's Name **Al-ʿAzīz**. Al-ʿUzzā was a tree on which the idolaters had placed a monument and curtains, in the area of Nakhlah, between Makkah and At-Tā'if. The Quraysh revered Al-ʿUzzā.

This is the idol that was shouted at the Muslims on a battlefield. During the battle of Uhud, Abū Sufyān said, "We have Al-ʿUzzā, but you do not have Al-ʿUzzā." Allah's Messenger ﷺ replied:

> **قُولُوا: اللهُ مَوْلَانَا وَلَا مَوْلَى لَكُمْ**
> *"Say: Allah is our Supporter, but you have no support."*

Notice the shape of the reply. He ﷺ did not counter one talisman with another. He answered a *thing they possessed* with a *Lord who supports*, and told them plainly that on their side of the field there was no supporter at all. That is the argument of ayah 23 spoken in the middle of a battle.

### Manāt (ayah 20)

Manāt was another idol, in the area of Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Al-Madīnah. The tribes of Khuzāʿah, Aws and Khazraj used to revere it during the time of Jāhiliyyah, and they used to announce Hajj to the Ka'bah from next to Manāt — Al-Bukhārī collected a statement from ʿĀ'ishah with this meaning. Muhammad ibn Ishāq said Manāt was the idol of the Aws and Khazraj tribes and those who followed their religion in Yathrib (Al-Madīnah). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, reports the tribal attributions a little differently: Lāt for the tribe of Thaqīf or the residents of Tā'if, ʿUzzā for the Quraysh, and Manāt for Banū Hilāl. The scholars transmit these associations with some variation; what none of them disputes is the fame of the three.

Ayah 20 calls Manāt **"the third one, the other"**. The phrasing lands almost dismissively — as though after two, a third is simply one more in a list that could be extended. And it could: Ibn Kathir goes on to name Dhul-Khalasah, the idol of Daws, Khathʿam and Bajīlah and the Arabs living in Tabalah — which, he says, was called the Southern Ka'bah, while the Ka'bah in Makkah was called the Northern Ka'bah — and Fals, the idol of Tayy; Riyām, a house of worship in Sanʿā'; Ruḍā', a structure of Banū Rabīʿah; and Dhul-Kaʿbāt in Sindād, the idol of Bakr and Taghlib. A whole map of sanctuaries. Ayah 23 dissolves every one of them in a single sentence.

## Ayat 21–22: the division that shames them

**"Do you have sons while He has daughters? Then this is a biased distribution!"**

Ibn Kathir puts the argument as a direct question to the idolaters: *do you choose female offspring for Allah and give preference to yourselves with the males?* They regarded daughters as the lesser share — and then assigned that lesser share to their Lord while keeping the better portion for themselves.

Then comes the sting. Ibn Kathir says: if you made this division between yourselves and the created, it would already be **قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ** — an unfair and unjust division. "How is it then that you make this division between you and Allah, even though this would be foolish and unjust, if you made it between yourselves and others?"

**The word ḍīzā.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ḍīzā* means to act or behave unjustly, or to defraud someone of their right or their due; Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās accordingly interprets the phrase as an unjust or unfair division. So the charge is not merely that their logic is poor. It is put in the language of *defrauding* — short-changing Allah of what they imagine is His while pocketing the better share themselves.

There is a double condemnation folded in here. Allah is far removed from what they ascribe to Him; and inside that falsehood they manage to insult Him again by the terms of the split. Ibn Kathir describes what Allah is refuting as "innovated lies, falsehood and atheism they invented through worshipping the idols and calling them gods."

## Ayah 23: the verdict — "mere names"

**إِنْ هِيَ إِلَّا أَسْمَاءٌ سَمَّيْتُمُوهَا أَنْتُمْ وَآبَاؤُكُمْ**
*"These are mere names that you and your forefathers have named…"*

This is the centre of gravity of the passage. Everything before it — the white stone, the tree at Nakhlah, the shrine at Mushallal, the curtains, the custodians, the tribal boasting, the battlefield slogan — is reduced to a single category: **naming**. There is a name, and behind the name, nothing. Ibn Kathir adds that the naming was done "of your own desire" — the label came from within them, never from above.

The ayah then closes off every route of appeal.

**"…for which Allah has sent down no authority."** *Sultān* here, Ibn Kathir explains, means **proof**. And notice the verb: *sent down*. The only currency that counts in the question of who deserves worship is what comes down from Allah. Antiquity does not count. Tribal consensus does not count. The grandeur of the sanctuary does not count. If it did not come down from Him, it is not evidence.

**"They follow but a guess, and that which they themselves desire."** Ibn Kathir strips out what was actually holding the whole system up: they had no proof, except their trust in their forefathers who took this false path in the past, as well as their lusts and their desire to become leaders, and thereby gain honour and reverence for their forefathers. Guesswork on the surface; self-interest underneath. A religion that flatters your standing and asks nothing of your evidence is one you will defend fiercely and examine never.

**A note on the word ẓann (guess/conjecture).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its careful discussion of this word a few verses further on, at the phrase *"and conjecture is of no use in the matter of Truth"* (53:28) — but since the same word appears here in ayah 23, the distinction it draws is worth knowing, and it belongs to that later verse rather than to this one. There, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ẓann* carries several senses in Arabic. One is baseless thoughts. Another sets *ẓann* against *yaqīn* — assured, definitive knowledge about something that really exists and is not a figment of the imagination, leaving no room for doubt, as with knowledge gained from the Qur'an and from Prophetic traditions reported by so many people that their agreeing upon a falsehood is impossible. A third sense is knowledge that *does* rest on a proof, only a proof not so certain as to rule out other possibilities — for example, injunctions based on general narrations of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. Rulings of the first sort are called *qaṭʿiyyāt* or *yaqīniyyāt*; those of the second, *ẓanniyyāt*. That second kind is recognised by the Sharīʿah, there is ample evidence for it in the Qur'an and Sunnah, and the entire Ummah concurs that acting upon it is obligatory. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion at that verse is that when the verse denounces *ẓann*, it means the first type — baseless thoughts — and so there is no contradiction.

**"…whereas there has surely come to them the guidance from their Lord."** This is what turns the ayah from a description into a rebuke. Ibn Kathir: Allah has sent them Messengers with the clear truth and unequivocal evidence — however, they did not adhere to or follow the guidance that came to them through the Prophets. Guidance was not withheld from them and then demanded of them. It arrived, and they preferred the guess.

## How the story ended

The three names had no future. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that after the conquest of Makkah the Holy Prophet ﷺ demolished them, and Ibn Kathir supplies the detail.

An-Nasā'ī recorded that Abū At-Tufayl said that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, he sent Khālid ibn Al-Walīd to the area of Nakhlah, where the idol of Al-ʿUzzā was erected on three trees of a forest. Khālid cut the three trees, approached the house built around it and destroyed it, then went back and informed the Prophet ﷺ of the story. The Prophet ﷺ said to him:

> **ارْجِعْ فَإِنَّكَ لَمْ تَصْنَعْ شَيْئًا**
> *"Go back and finish your mission, for you have not finished it."*

Khālid went back. When the custodians, who were also its servants, saw him, they started calling upon Al-ʿUzzā. When Khālid approached it he found a naked woman whose hair was untidy and who was throwing sand on her head, and he killed her with the sword. When he returned, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: **"That was Al-ʿUzzā!"** The idol the Quraysh revered, whose name had been shouted across the field at Uhud, was that — and once it was gone, the trees were felled and the house around it was rubble. The name had never had anything behind it.

Ibn Kathir adds that the Prophet ﷺ sent Al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah and Abū Sufyān Sakhr ibn Harb to destroy Al-Lāt; they carried out his command and built a masjid in its place in the city of At-Tā'if — the house of a name replaced by a house for the worship of Allah. To demolish Manāt he ﷺ sent Abū Sufyān Sakhr ibn Harb or ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullah Al-Bajalī to Dhul-Khalasah and he destroyed it; and Ibn Hishām said that some people of knowledge told him that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib to Fals, and he destroyed it.

## What this asks of us

**Test the name against the evidence.** The argument of ayah 23 is not "your gods are weak" but "your gods are *nothing* — you named them." The question it trains a believer to ask of anything claiming his devotion is simply: *what did Allah send down about this?* If the honest answer is inherited practice, communal pride, or a strong feeling, the ayah has already answered it.

**Watch the two roots of falsehood.** Ibn Kathir names them precisely: trust in forefathers who took a false path, and the appetites of the self. Respect for those who came before us is natural and often good — but the moment it becomes the *reason* for a religious belief, it has taken the place that proof should occupy. Desire is subtler still: Ibn Kathir mentions the desire to become leaders. It is worth asking honestly what we ourselves gain from a position we defend loudly.

**Beware the slide that made Al-Lāt.** A man who served the pilgrims became a grave people stayed beside, and then a stone people worshipped. No one in that chain set out to commit shirk. Honour the righteous by following them, and keep worship — every part of it — for Allah alone.

**And remember the answer given at Uhud.** When the world holds up its names and asks what you have, the reply the Prophet ﷺ taught is not a rival name: *Allah is our Supporter, and you have no support.*

passages.title: Wishes, intercession, and naming the angels
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat finish the Qur'an's demolition of Makkan idolatry by going after the two things Ibn Kathir says were holding it up: **what people merely wished were true**, and **what people had merely named** without proof. Ayah 24 addresses wishful thinking, ayah 25 states who actually owns both worlds, ayah 26 removes the imagined safety net of intercession, and ayat 27–28 expose the whole edifice as names and guesswork. The thread running through them is a single question: on what authority do you believe what you believe?

## The argument these ayat complete

Just before this, in ayat 19–23, Allah had named the three great idols of the Arabs. Ibn Kathir describes them in detail. **Al-Lāt** was a white stone with inscriptions on it, with a house built around it at aṭ-Ṭāʾif with curtains, servants and a sacred courtyard; the people of aṭ-Ṭāʾif, the tribe of Thaqīf and their allies worshipped it, and they used to boast about having it to the Arabs, except the Quraysh. **Al-ʿUzzā** was a tree at Nakhlah, between Makkah and aṭ-Ṭāʾif, on which the idolaters had placed a monument and curtains; the Quraysh revered it. **Manāt** stood at Mushallal near Qudayd, between Makkah and Madinah, revered by Khuzāʿah, Aws and Khazraj, who used to announce Hajj to the Kaʿbah from next to it. Ibn Kathir notes the fundamental imitation at work: "They built houses for their idols to resemble the Kaʿbah built by Prophet Ibrāhīm."

Even the names were borrowed. Ibn Jarīr said the Arabs derived *Al-Lāt* from the Name of Allah, and made it feminine — "Allah is far removed from what they ascribe to Him" — and that they likewise derived the name of *Al-ʿUzzā* from His Name *Al-ʿAzīz*.

Ibn Jarīr also reports, on the authority of ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, that Al-Lāt had been a man who used to mix *sawīq* (a kind of barley mash) with water for the pilgrims in the time of Jāhiliyyah; when he died, they remained next to his grave and worshipped him. Separately, Al-Bukhārī recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said, commenting on the words *"Al-Lāt, and Al-ʿUzzā"*: **"Al-Lāt was a man who used to mix sawīq for the pilgrims."** (Two reports, and it is worth keeping them apart: the grave detail comes through Ibn Jarīr's report, not through the words Al-Bukhārī records.)

Then came the verdict in ayah 23: **"They are but names which you have named — you and your fathers — for which Allah has sent down no authority."** Ibn Kathir explains *sulṭān* here as **proof**. And on the words "They follow but a guess and that which they themselves desire," he identifies what was actually driving the system: "they have no proof, except their trust in their forefathers who took this false path in the past, as well as their lusts and desires to become leaders, and thereby gain honour and reverence for their forefathers" — inherited guesswork and personal appetite, "whereas there has surely come to them the guidance from their Lord."

Those same two things reappear in what follows: **wishing** in ayah 24, and **conjecture** in ayah 28.

## Ayah 24 — wishing does not make it so

**أَمْ لِلْإِنسَانِ مَا تَمَنَّىٰ** — *"Or shall man have what he wishes?"*

Ibn Kathir reads the question as a denial: it is "asserting that not everyone gets the goodness that he wishes." He brings a verse that turns the point directly on the believing community:

> **"It will not be in accordance with desires (of Muslims), nor those of the People of Scripture."** (4:123)

His summary is worth memorising: **"not everyone who claims to be guided is truly guided, and not everyone gets what he wishes for himself."** That is a devastating line, because the ayah is aimed first at pagans who imagined the idols would sort things out for them — but as Ibn Kathir applies it, the principle does not stop there. Claiming a thing is not the same as being it, and wanting an outcome is not the same as being given it.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith that Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"When one of you wishes for something, let him be careful with what he wishes for, because he does not know what part of his wish will be written for him."**

Ibn Kathir notes: "Only Ahmad collected this Hadith." Notice that the hadith uses the very verb of the ayah — **تَمَنَّىٰ (tamannā)**, to wish. A wish is not harmless daydreaming. Some part of it may in fact be written for you, and the Prophet ﷺ told us to look carefully at what we are asking for.

## Ayah 25 — both houses belong to Allah

**فَلِلَّهِ الْآخِرَةُ وَالْأُولَىٰ** — *"But to Allah belongs the last (the Hereafter) and the first (this world)."*

Ibn Kathir: "all matters belong to Allah and He is the King and Owner of this world and the Hereafter, Who does what He will in both lives. **Whatever He wills, occurs and whatever He does not will, never occurs.**"

That is why wishing has no purchase. Neither of the two houses is ours. We do not own the outcomes of this life, and we certainly do not own the outcomes of the next; both belong to the One who does what He wills in both.

## Ayah 26 — even the angels cannot act on their own

**وَكَم مِّن مَّلَكٍ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ لَا تُغْنِي شَفَاعَتُهُمْ شَيْئًا إِلَّا مِن بَعْدِ أَن يَأْذَنَ اللَّهُ لِمَن يَشَاءُ وَيَرْضَىٰ**

*"And there are many angels in the heavens, whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah has given leave for whom He wills and is pleased with."*

Read the exceptive clause slowly, because every word narrows the gate:
- **إِلَّا مِن بَعْدِ أَن يَأْذَنَ اللَّهُ** — "except *after* Allah has given leave."
- **لِمَن يَشَاءُ** — the leave is for whom He wills.
- **وَيَرْضَىٰ** — and it goes with His good pleasure.

Ibn Kathir places the ayah alongside two others that say the same thing:

> **"Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?"** (2:255)

> **"Intercession with Him profits not except for him whom He permits."** (34:23)

Then he drives home the argument from the greater to the lesser: **"If this is the case with the angels who are close to Him, how can you, O ignorant ones, hope for Allah to grant you the intercession of the idols and rivals you worship with Him without having His permission or any divine legislation permitting you to worship them? Rather, Allah has forbidden idol worshipping by the tongues of all of His Messengers and He revealed this prohibition in all of His Books."**

That is the whole force of the ayah for a worshipper. The idolatrous business model was: attach yourself to a shrine, and it will speak for you. Ayah 26 cuts the wire. If the mightiest, nearest creatures — the angels — do not benefit anyone by intercession except after Allah's leave, a stone at aṭ-Ṭāʾif or a tree at Nakhlah certainly cannot. And the ayah names the condition it does hold out: Allah's **leave**, and His **pleasure**.

## Ayat 27–28 — the naming, and the guesswork behind it

**إِنَّ الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ لَيُسَمُّونَ الْمَلَائِكَةَ …** — *"Verily, those who believe not in the Hereafter name the angels with female names."*

Ibn Kathir: "Allah the Exalted admonishes the idolators for calling the angels female names and claiming that they are Allah's daughters. **Allah is far removed from what they ascribe to Him.**" Note what has happened. It is no longer only invented names for invented gods; now real creatures of Allah have a false description hung on them.

He brings a parallel verse, which asks the one question that ends the argument:

> **"And they make females the angels, who themselves are servants of the Most Gracious. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned!"** (43:19)

Two things there. First, the angels are described as **servants of the Most Gracious** — the very status the idolaters were denying them by turning them into divine offspring. Second, the challenge: *were you there?* And such speech is **testimony** — it is written down, and they will be questioned about it.

Notice, too, whom ayah 27 names: **those who do not believe in the Hereafter**. That is the description Allah attaches to the people who speak this way about His angels.

Ayah 28 then states the void where their evidence should be: **وَمَا لَهُم بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ** — *"But they have no knowledge thereof."* Ibn Kathir: "they have no correct knowledge testifying to their statements. What they say is all lies, falsehood, fake and utter atheism." And then: **إِن يَتَّبِعُونَ إِلَّا الظَّنَّ ۖ وَإِنَّ الظَّنَّ لَا يُغْنِي مِنَ الْحَقِّ شَيْئًا** — *"They follow but conjecture, and verily, conjecture is no substitute for the truth"* — which he glosses: "conjecture is of no benefit and never takes the place of truth."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> **"Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most lying speech."**

The same word — **ẓann** — that ruins a person's theology also ruins his dealings with other people.

## What exactly is being condemned? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān on *ẓann*

This matters, because a reader might conclude from ayah 28 that any belief short of absolute certainty is blameworthy — which would gut Islamic law itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān heads this off by distinguishing the senses of **ظَنّ (ẓann)**:

1. **Baseless thought** — an idea with nothing under it at all. "This is the sense in which it is employed in the verse, because baseless thoughts were the cause of idolatry. And the verse purports to remove the cause."
2. **Ẓann as the opposite of yaqīn.** *Yaqīn* is "assured or definitive knowledge about something that really exists, not the figment of someone's imagination" — where there is no room for doubt or suspicion. The examples given: knowledge gained from the Qur'an, and from Prophetic Traditions reported uninterruptedly by so large a number of people that it is impossible they should agree upon falsehood.
3. **Ẓann as reasoned probability** — "knowledge that is based on a proof, and not on baseless thoughts, but the proof is not so certain as may rule out other possibilities," such as injunctions based on general narrations of the Prophet ﷺ.

Rulings of the first certainty-grade are called **qaṭʿiyyāt** or **yaqīniyyāt**; those of the third are called **ẓanniyyāt**. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: "This type of Zann is recognized by Sharīʿah. There is ample evidence in Qur'an and Sunnah of its recognition. **The entire Ummah concurs that it is obligatory to act upon it.**" The ayah, when it denounces *ẓann*, "refers to the first type … which connotes baseless thoughts. **Thus there is no contradiction.**"

So the passage is not an attack on careful reasoning from evidence. It is an attack on the mind that asserts without any evidence at all — and then builds a religion on the assertion.

## Living it

**Ask what your certainty is standing on.** When the idolaters were asked for *sulṭān* — proof — Ibn Kathir says what they actually had was trust in their forefathers plus an appetite for leadership and honour. Both are still in circulation.

**Watch what you wish for.** Ayah 24 and the hadith recorded by Ahmad together: not everyone gets what he wishes for himself, and part of your wish may be written for you — so look carefully at what you are asking for. Aim your wishes at what you would still want in the world that ayah 25 says Allah owns: the last as well as the first.

**Do not shop for intermediaries.** If the angels' intercession avails nothing except after Allah's leave, no shrine or object has standing of its own. The ayah names Allah's leave and Allah's pleasure as the terms — so put your effort there.

**Guard your speech about what you do not know** — about Allah, about the unseen, and about people. The verse Ibn Kathir cites (43:19) calls such speech testimony that will be recorded and asked about; and the Prophet ﷺ warned us against suspicion, "for suspicion is the most lying speech."

passages.title: Turn from the heedless; the reckoning is His
