These four ayat close the argument that began with the idolaters' guesswork about the angels, and they do it by shifting the ground entirely. Instead of continuing to argue, Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ to withdraw from a certain kind of person — and then explains why that withdrawal is safe: the heavens and the earth belong to Allah, the reckoning is His, and He alone knows who is truly guided. What holds ayat 29–32 together is that single movement, from *stop arguing with them* to *the accounting is not yours to run*.

## The command in ayah 29: turn away

The immediately preceding ayah said of the idolaters that "they follow but conjecture, and verily, conjecture is no substitute for the truth." Ibn Kathir explains that they had no sound knowledge behind their claim that the angels were Allah's daughters — "what they say is all lies, falsehood, fake and utter atheism" — and that *ẓann*, conjecture, "is of no benefit and never takes the place of truth." He cites here a hadith recorded in the Sahih in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most lying speech."

That is the setting for ayah 29: **فَأَعْرِضْ عَن مَّن تَوَلَّىٰ عَن ذِكْرِنَا** — "Therefore withdraw from him who turns away from Our Reminder."

Ibn Kathir's gloss is direct: it means "stay away from those who turn away from the Truth and shun them." He gives this section of his commentary a heading that captures the weight of it — *The Necessity of turning away from the People of Misguidance*.

Notice how carefully the ayah draws the person it is describing. This is not someone who simply has not yet heard. It is someone who has met the Reminder and turned away from it, and who — as the rest of the ayah says — wants nothing beyond this world. The command is about that person.

## "And desires nothing but the life of this world"

The ayah then gives the diagnosis: **وَلَمْ يُرِدْ إِلَّا الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا** — "and desires nothing but the life of this world." Ibn Kathir reads this as describing someone "whose aim and knowledge are concentrated on this life," and he adds a hard sentence: "this is the goal of those who have no goodness in them."

What Ibn Kathir puts his finger on is where a person's *aim* comes to rest. The whole horizon of this man's wanting stops at this world; nothing beyond it is what he is actually after.

## Ayah 30: "That is the extent of their knowledge"

**ذَٰلِكَ مَبْلَغُهُم مِّنَ الْعِلْمِ** — "That is what they could reach of knowledge."

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase: "seeking this life and striving hard in its affairs is the best knowledge they have acquired." Read carefully, that is a devastating verdict, and precisely not because it calls them incapable. Ibn Kathir grants them striving, effort, hard work in worldly affairs — and says that *this* is the best knowledge they ever managed to reach. All of that capability terminates at a ceiling, and the ceiling is this world.

Ibn Kathir attaches to this a reported supplication:

> *O Allah! Make not this life the greatest of our concerns nor the best knowledge that we can attain.*

The supplication picks up the ayah's own words — مَبْلَغَ عِلْمِنَا, the extent of our knowledge — and turns them into a prayer for protection. That is the most practical thing a believer can do with ayah 30: pray not to be described by it.

**A warning for us, not only for them.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refuses to let this ayah stay in the past. It observes that the Qur'an here describes the condition of those unbelievers who denied the Hereafter and the Day of Judgment, and then adds, with real grief, that nowadays the Muslims have characterised themselves by the same condition, as a result of Western education and material needs and desires: all our attempts to progress in the various branches of knowledge, sciences and arts pivot on economics, and we do not think even by mistake about matters relating to the Hereafter. We believe in the Holy Prophet ﷺ and hope for his intercession — yet Allah commands that very Prophet ﷺ to withdraw from the people of misguidance and shun them. The commentary ends the point with a plea: we seek refuge in Allah from such misguidance.

## "Your Lord knows best who has strayed"

The second half of ayah 30 explains why the Prophet ﷺ can afford to turn away: **إِنَّ رَبَّكَ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَن ضَلَّ عَن سَبِيلِهِ وَهُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنِ اهْتَدَىٰ** — "Verily, your Lord is He, Who knows best him who goes astray from His path, and He knows best him who receives guidance."

Ibn Kathir: He is the Creator of all creatures and He knows whatever benefits His servants. Allah is the One Who guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, and all of this indicates His power, knowledge and wisdom. Ibn Kathir then closes the door on any misreading: "Certainly, He is Just and never legislates or decrees unjustly."

Two things are being lifted off the Prophet's ﷺ shoulders here — and off ours. The verdict on a heart is not our department, and neither is the guidance. Both belong, as Ibn Kathir says, to the Creator who knows what benefits His servants.

## Ayah 31: why the reckoning is His

**وَلِلَّهِ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ** — "And to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth."

Ibn Kathir draws out what this ownership establishes: Allah is the King and Owner of the heavens and the earth; He is independent of the need for anyone; He is the authority over His creation and rules them with justice; and He created the creation in truth.

Ownership is stated as the ground of the judgment — the ayah continues with a purpose clause, *li-yajziya*, "so that He may requite":

> **لِيَجْزِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسَاءُوا بِمَا عَمِلُوا وَيَجْزِيَ الَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا بِالْحُسْنَىٰ**
> "…that He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done, and reward those who do good, with what is best."

Ibn Kathir summarises: "He recompenses each according to his or her deeds, good for good and evil for evil." And the two halves are worded differently in the ayah itself. The evildoer is repaid **بِمَا عَمِلُوا**, with that which they have done. The good-doer is repaid **بِالْحُسْنَىٰ**, with what is best.

## Ayah 32: who exactly are "those who do good"?

Ayah 31 promised the best to *those who do good*. Ayah 32 immediately tells us who they are, and the definition is startlingly merciful:

**الَّذِينَ يَجْتَنِبُونَ كَبَائِرَ الْإِثْمِ وَالْفَوَاحِشَ إِلَّا اللَّمَمَ** — "Those who avoid great sins and *al-fawāḥish* (immoral sins), except *al-lamam*."

Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: the good-doers are those who avoid major sins and immoral sins; they sometimes commit minor sins, but they will be forgiven these and covered from exposure. He links this to Allah's promise in another ayah: "If you avoid the great sins which you are forbidden to do, We shall expiate from you your (small) sins, and admit you to a Noble Entrance" (4:31). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point about the exception: they do sometimes commit minor sins, and that does not exclude them from the category of the *muḥsinīn*, the good-doers.

### What is *al-lamam*?

Ibn Kathir states it briefly: *al-lamam* means small faults and minor errors. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the Companions and those who followed them interpreted the word in two different ways:

**1. Small faults and minor errors** — what Sūrah an-Nisāʾ calls *sayyi'āt*, the minor sins that 4:31 promises to write off for whoever avoids the major ones. Maʿārif notes that Ibn Kathir reported this from Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Hurayrah.

**2. A sin a person commits incidentally and then repents from**, never repeating it afterwards. Maʿārif notes that Ibn Kathir reported a narration from Ibn Jarir — first through Mujāhid, and again through ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and through Ḥasan al-Baṣrī from Abū Hurayrah. The gist, Maʿārif says, is that even someone who commits a major sin incidentally and repents will not be excluded from the ranks of those mindful of Allah. Maʿārif cites 3:135 in support: those who, when they happen to commit a shameful act or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness — "and who is there to forgive sins except Allah?" — and do not persist in what they have done, knowingly.

**The safeguard.** Maʿārif adds that the overwhelming majority of scholars concur that if a person persists in a minor sin and continues doing it in a determined way until it becomes a habit, it is no longer a minor sin but has turned into a major one. On that basis Maulānā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī explained *lamam* as those small sins **in which the doer does not persist**. That one qualification protects the ayah from being read as permission.

**Ibn ʿAbbās's illustration.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying: "I have not seen anything that resembles *al-lamam* better than the hadith that Abū Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ" — that Allah the Exalted has decreed for the son of Adam his share of *zinā* and he will certainly earn his share; the *zinā* of the eye is by looking, the *zinā* of the tongue is by talking, and the heart wishes and lusts, but the sexual organ either substantiates all this or not. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs. Ibn Jarir recorded Ibn Masʿūd saying much the same — the eyes commit *zinā* by looking, the lips by kissing, the hands by transgressing, the feet by walking — and that when the act itself is not committed, "it is *al-lamam*." Masrūq and ash-Shaʿbī also held this view. And when ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Nāfiʿ, known as Ibn Lubābah aṭ-Ṭāʾifī, asked Abū Hurayrah about "except the *lamam*," he answered that it pertains to kissing, winking one's eye, looking and embracing — while the act of intercourse itself is *zinā*.

Taken together with Thānawī's qualification, *lamam* names the near-misses and small failures of a person who is genuinely trying, not the settled habits of a person who is not.

## "Your Lord is of vast forgiveness"

**إِنَّ رَبَّكَ وَاسِعُ الْمَغْفِرَةِ.** Ibn Kathir: this asserts that His mercy encompasses everything, and His forgiveness entails every type of sin, if one repents. He quotes: "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves! Despair not of the mercy of Allah: verily, Allah forgives all sins. Truly, He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (39:53).

Read in sequence, the ayah is beautifully balanced: minor slips are covered for the one who avoids the majors — and beyond that, no type of sin at all is outside His forgiveness for the one who repents.

## "He knows you best" — the argument against self-congratulation

**هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِكُمْ إِذْ أَنشَأَكُم مِّنَ الْأَرْضِ وَإِذْ أَنتُمْ أَجِنَّةٌ فِي بُطُونِ أُمَّهَاتِكُمْ** — "He knows you well when He created you from the earth, and when you were fetuses in your mothers' wombs."

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah was and still is the All-Knowing, whose knowledge encompasses your affairs, your statements and all the actions that will be committed by you — already when He created your father Adam from the earth and took his offspring from his loin, as small as ants, then divided them into two groups, a group destined for Paradise and a group for the Fire. And "when you were fetuses in your mothers' wombs" refers to when He commanded the angel to record one's provisions, age, actions, and whether he would be among the miserable or the happy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the human lesson out of this. *Ajinnah* is the plural of *janīn*, an embryo or foetus. The point, Maʿārif says, is that a person does not have knowledge of himself as much as Allah knows him: while he was going through the various phases of his creation in his mother's womb he had no knowledge and no sense at all — but his Creator knew fully well how wisely He was creating him. From this a person is made aware of his own inability and lack of sufficient knowledge; and then of a second thing, that any good he does is not his personal accomplishment. It is Allah who gave him limbs, organs and other parts of the body to perform righteous deeds; He who equipped him with the ability to move them; He who created the urge, the will and the determination to perform righteous actions. Hence, Maʿārif concludes, not even the greatest righteous, pious and devout person has the right to take pride in his works. Besides, no one yet knows what the end result of his activities will be — and that end result is the most important factor of all. Pride and arrogance, on that accounting, are simply meaningless.

## "So do not claim purity for yourselves"

**فَلَا تُزَكُّوا أَنفُسَكُمْ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنِ اتَّقَىٰ** — "So, ascribe not purity to yourselves. He knows best him who has taqwa."

Ibn Kathir: this forbids a person from ascribing purity to himself, praising himself, and thinking highly of his own actions. He cites: "Have you not seen those who claim sanctity for themselves. Nay, but Allah sanctifies whom He wills, and they will not be dealt with unjustly, even equal to the extent of a *fatīl*" (4:49).

The Sunnah then shows how seriously this was taken in practice:

- **In his Sahih, Muslim recorded** that Muhammad bin ʿAmr bin ʿAṭāʾ said: "I called my daughter Barrah (the pious one), and Zaynab bint Abū Salamah said to me, 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade using this name. I was originally called Barrah,' and he ﷺ said: 'Do not ascribe purity to yourselves; Allah knows best who the pious people among you are.'" They asked what she should be called, and he ﷺ said: "Call her Zaynab." (Maʿārif adds that the Prophet ﷺ recited this very phrase of the ayah — *fa-lā tuzakkū anfusakum* — when he suggested the change.)
- **Imam Ahmad recorded** from ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Abī Bakrah, from his father, that a man praised another man before the Prophet ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Woe to you, you have cut off the neck of your friend!" — repeating it — "If one of you must praise a friend of his, let him say: I think that so-and-so is this and that; Allah knows best about him and I will never purify anyone before Allah," and this only if he knows his friend to be as he is describing him. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah collected this hadith.
- **Imam Ahmad recorded** that Hammām bin al-Ḥārith said: "A man came before ʿUthmān bin ʿAffān and praised him. Al-Miqdād bin al-Aswad started throwing sand in the face of that man, saying, 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered us to throw sand in their faces when we see those who praise.'" Muslim and Abu Dawud also collected this hadith.

Maʿārif sums up the closing phrase: the merit of a person lies not only in his outward actions, but in the *taqwa* in his heart and in his inner moral excellence and uprightness — the kind that endures until his death. Only Allah knows who is perfect in that quality.

## Living it

- **Know when the conversation is over.** Ayah 29 commands the Prophet ﷺ to withdraw from the one who has turned away from the Reminder and wants nothing but this world. Ibn Kathir titles it a *necessity*. Withdrawing there is not failure; it is obedience.
- **Watch your ceiling.** Ayah 30 asks a searching question: is worldly striving the best knowledge I ever attain? Make the reported supplication your own — that this life not be the greatest of your concerns nor the best knowledge you reach.
- **Aim at the majors.** Ayah 32 does not demand flawlessness. It asks you to avoid the great sins and the shameful acts, to refuse to make a habit of the small ones, and to repent when you slip.
- **Never despair, and never boast.** The same ayah that says "your Lord is of vast forgiveness" ends with "ascribe not purity to yourselves." Hope in His mercy; suspend judgment on your own standing — and on everyone else's, since He knows best who truly fears Him.

passages.title: The man who withheld, and what the scrolls say
passages.tafsir:
A man is shown to us who began to move towards faith, paid something to buy his way out of the consequences, and then stopped short. Against that small, calculating figure Allah sets Ibrāhīm — the man who *fulfilled* — and then quotes what stands written in the scrolls of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm: no one carries anyone else's load. What holds ayat 33–42 together is one question about accountability: can responsibility be transferred? The answer is no, twice over — not your sins onto someone else, and not someone else's righteousness onto you.

## The incident behind the words

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from *Ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr* on the authority of Ibn Jarīr, that a man embraced Islam and one of his friends rebuked him for abandoning the religion of his forefathers. The man answered that he feared Allah's chastisement. So the friend made him an offer: pay me a certain sum, and I will take your punishment in the Hereafter upon myself — you will be spared. The man paid. The friend then demanded more. After a scuffle he paid the additional amount, and for the outstanding balance a document was drawn up and witnessed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing *Rūḥ-ul-Maʿānī*, that the man inclined towards Islam was Walīd ibn Mughīrah, whose friend reproached him and took the responsibility of punishment onto his own shoulders.

Hold that image while you read ayat 33–34: a man walking away from faith with a receipt in his hand. Everything that follows dismantles that transaction.

## Ayah 33 — "the one who turned away"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *tawallā* literally means to turn the face away; here it means one who turns away from the obedience of Allah — a bodily word before it is a moral one. Ibn Kathīr places the ayah among verses in which Allah chastises those who turn from His obedience: *"So he neither believed nor prayed! But on the contrary, he belied and turned away!"* (75:31–32).

## Ayah 34 — the word that means "he hit rock"

*Wa aʿṭā qalīlan wa akdā* — "and gave a little, then stopped."

The whole ayah turns on *akdā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it derives from *kudyah*: the hard, stony ground or clod that turns up while a man is digging a well or a trench, so that he can dig no further. ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, draw the same picture: "Like the case of a people who dig a well, during the course of which they find a rock preventing them from completing their work. So they say, 'We are finished' and they abandon the work."

That is the shape of this man's soul: he broke ground, went down a little way, struck something harder than he had budgeted for, and called it a day.

Ibn Kathīr records that Ibn ʿAbbās read the ayah as "Gave a little, then stopped giving," and that Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and several others said the like. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the two readings side by side: with the incident above in view the meaning is transparent — he paid a small amount and then stopped payment; apart from that, the same early authorities take it of anyone who spends a little in the way of Allah and then stops, or who inclines towards Allah's obedience, obeys Him for a while, and then gives it up. So the ayah has a wide door: a specific Makkan bargain, and also the giving that dries up and the religious enthusiasm that runs out of road.

## Ayah 35 — "Does he have knowledge of the Unseen?"

*A ʿindahu ʿilmu-l-ghaybi fa huwa yarā* — a question that expects no answer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it two applications. Following the occasion of revelation: the man abandoned Islam because a friend assured him he would carry his punishment, and he took that guarantee for granted. Does he then have knowledge of the Unseen, so that he can actually *see* that the chastisement he has earned will certainly be taken over by his friend? It is, in Maʿārif's words, wholly a make-believe situation — he has no such knowledge, and his friend can neither assume another man's punishment nor save him from it.

Apart from that story, both Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān read it of the man who stops giving out of fear of poverty: does he possess knowledge of the Unseen, and therefore know that if he does not stop spending his wealth will be depleted and not replenished? No. Such a person stopped his charity for righteous causes and cut off his kinsfolk out of miserliness, stinginess, and fear of poverty.

Notice what is exposed: miserliness is a *claim to knowledge* — the withholder quietly asserts that he reads the future ledger better than his Lord does. Ibn Kathīr answers with the Prophet's ﷺ words to Bilāl — spend, and do not fear that the Owner of the Throne will give you less — and with Allah's promise: *"And whatsoever you spend of anything, He will replace it. And He is the Best of providers"* (34:39).

## Ayat 36–37 — the scrolls of Mūsā, and Ibrāhīm "who fulfilled"

The rebuke now shifts from his purse to his ignorance: has he not been told what stands in the *ṣuḥuf* — the scrolls, the written pages — of Mūsā, and of Ibrāhīm, *alladhī waffā*?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *waffā* from the root *wafāʼ*: to fulfil faithfully a covenant one has made. Ibrāhīm عليه السلام had a covenant with Allah that he would obey Him and convey His message to all people, and he honoured it — and was made to pass through severe trials and tribulations as a result. This, it notes, is the interpretation of Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Kathīr and others.

Ibn Kathīr gathers the early statements on the word:

- **Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Ath-Thawrī:** "Conveyed all that he was ordered to convey."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās:** "He delivered all that Allah ordered him to deliver."
- **Qatādah:** "He obeyed Allah and delivered His message to His creatures."

Ibn Kathīr notes that Qatādah's wording is the one Ibn Jarīr preferred, because it takes in the statements before it and supports them, and reads the title in the light of *"And when the Lord of Ibrahim tried him with certain commands, which he fulfilled. He said: 'Verily, I am going to make you an Imam for mankind'"* (2:124): Ibrāhīm fulfilled every command of his Lord, kept away from every prohibition, and conveyed Allah's message in its entirety — which is precisely why he is fit to be a leader for mankind in all his affairs, words and deeds. Hence the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ himself: *"Follow the religion of Ibrahim, a Ḥanīf, and he was not of the idolators"* (16:123).

**The narrower explanations.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that several narrations single out one particular practice of Ibrāhīm عليه السلام as the sense of *waffā*, and stresses that these do not contradict the broad meaning, since fulfilment of the covenant is general — it takes in acting on all the divine injunctions, obeying Allah in every action, discharging the duties of prophethood and messengership, and reforming Allah's creation. Among them:

- Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports from Abū Umāmah رضي الله عنه that the Prophet ﷺ recited ayah 37 and asked, "Do you know what *waffā* means?" Abū Umāmah replied, "Allah and His Messenger know best." The Prophet ﷺ said: "He fulfilled the day's work by starting it with the performance of four rakʿat" — that is, ṣalāt al-ishrāq, the prayer offered in the early part of the day.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this is supported by the tradition **recorded in Tirmidhī** on the authority of Abū Dharr رضي الله عنه, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "O son of Ādam! Perform four rakʿat of prayer in the early part of the day, and I shall take care of you in all your affairs till the end of the day."
- Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reports from Muʿādh ibn Anas رضي الله عنه that the Prophet ﷺ asked why Allah gave Ibrāhīm عليه السلام the title *alladhī waffā*, and said it was because he used to recite this dhikr every morning and evening: *"So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning; and to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you come to noon."*

## Ayat 38–39 — the two laws quoted from the scrolls

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays down a principle here: whenever a command, statement, action or teaching of Allah is quoted in the Qurʼān from the scriptures of the earlier Prophets, it is binding on this Ummah to act upon it, unless there is an explicit text abrogating it. Of the teachings drawn from the scrolls of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm in the verses that follow, it observes, only two concern practical life — ayat 38 and 39 — while the rest advise, warn, and draw attention to the signs of Allah.

**Ayah 38 — no bearer of burden bears another's burden.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *wizr* originally means a burden: every person will have to carry his own wrongdoing, whether disbelief or sin, and no one else will carry it. Ibn Kathīr says the same and cites *"And if one heavily laden calls another to bear his load, nothing of it will be lifted even though he be near of kin"* (35:18). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells out the sting: on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of one will not be handed to another, nor will anyone have the option of paying for another's sin — which is exactly the guarantee the friend in the story sold, with witnesses, for cash.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also answers an old objection: the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar رضي الله عنه, **recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥain**, that the dead are punished because of the weeping and wailing of their family. Quoting *Mazharī*, it explains that this concerns one who himself used to wail over the dead and was in the habit of it, or who instructed his heirs to wail for him after his death — so he is punished for his own deed, not another's. Muhammad Taqi Usmani adds that weeping one cannot control is no sin in the Sharīʿah; what is prohibited is the formal, often artificial wailing customary in pre-Islamic Arabia — crying out loudly, inviting others to weep, slapping the face, tearing clothes, complaining of destiny.

**Ayah 39 — a man gets only what he strove for.** Ibn Kathīr states the symmetry plainly: just as no soul carries another's burden, so no soul benefits except from the good it earned for itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān works this out practically. No one can discharge another's obligation: if a man prays or fasts on someone else's behalf, that person remains liable; if a man believes on another's behalf, the other is not thereby a believer. Then the two apparent exceptions. In **Ḥajj-e-Badal** — sending someone to perform Ḥajj on your behalf, permitted when a physical constraint makes you unable to go yourself — the sender bears the expenses himself, so it is his own act, and his own reward. In **Zakāh**, appointing someone to pay on your behalf is itself the act of the one who appointed, not of the appointee. Neither case conflicts with ayah 39.

**Does this ayah cancel conveying reward to others?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here. What ayah 39 denies is that a person can discharge another's obligatory duties — faith, prayer, fasting — for him; it does not deny that a person may perform a voluntary good deed and offer its reward to someone else. There is ample textual evidence in the Sharīʿah that one may supplicate, give charity, or do any other good deed and convey its reward to others, and an overwhelming consensus of the Ummah on this — a point it attributes to Ibn Kathīr. Where the scholars genuinely differed: Imām Ash-Shāfiʿī رحمه الله held that the reward of reciting the Qurʼān cannot be conveyed to another, taking this ayah in its general sense and arguing that purely bodily acts of worship — prayer, fasting, recitation — cannot be passed on. Imām Abū Ḥanīfah رحمه الله and the majority of the leading jurists held it permissible, reasoning that just as one may make duʿāʼ for another and convey the reward of charity to him, so one may recite the Qurʼān and offer voluntary worship and convey that reward too. Qurṭubī, it adds, cites a large number of traditions showing that a believer does receive benefit from another's righteous acts, and *Tafsīr Mazharī* has collected the relevant narrations on *īṣāl-e-thawāb* here.

**Why these two rules, and why from Mūsā and Ibrāhīm?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests that although both rules stood in the Sharīʿah of all the Prophets, they are mentioned in connection with Mūsā and Ibrāhīm عليهما السلام probably because in their days an evil custom had taken deep root of killing the son in place of the father, or a father, brother, sister or other relative in place of the son. Their Sharīʿah abolished such customs of the Age of Ignorance.

## Ayah 40 — "and his striving will be seen"

Ibn Kathīr: this means on the Day of Resurrection, and he cites *"And say: 'Do deeds! Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be brought back to the All-Knower of the unseen and the seen. Then He will inform you of what you used to do'"* (9:105).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses on the inside of the deed: outer actions alone are not enough — Allah takes into account the real, inner motive and driving force behind them, whether they were done with sincerity of purpose or with some ulterior motive. It cites the Prophet's ﷺ well-known words that actions are judged only by intentions: deeds must be done purely for the pleasure of Allah and in compliance with His command.

## What Ibn Kathīr adds: the deeds that keep working

Because ayah 39 says a man has only what he strove for, Ibn Kathīr raises the hadith **recorded by Muslim in the Ṣaḥīḥ**, from Abū Hurayrah رضي الله عنه, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When a person dies, his deeds will cease except in three cases: from a righteous son who invokes Allah for him, or an ongoing charity after his death, or knowledge that people benefit from."

His resolution: these three are themselves the fruit of the man's own deeds, effort and action. A hadith states that the best provision a man consumes is what he himself has earned, and that his offspring are among what he has earned. The ongoing charity he leaves behind — an endowment, for instance — is among the traces of his own actions; and Allah says: *"Verily, We give life to the dead, and We record that which they send before them and their traces"* (36:12). The knowledge he spreads, by which people are guided, is likewise his own deed — and a hadith **collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ** states: "Whoever invites to guidance, he will earn as much reward as those who follow him, without decreasing anything out of their own rewards."

## Ayah 41 — the recompense in full

*Thumma yujzāhu-l-jazāʼa-l-awfā* — rendered in our sources as "Then he will be recompensed with a full and the best recompense." Ibn Kathīr: Allah will remind you of your actions and recompense you for them in the best manner — good for good, and evil for evil.

## Ayah 42 — "and that to your Lord is the ultimate end"

Ibn Kathīr: *ilā rabbika-l-muntahā* means the return of everything on the Day of Resurrection. He records, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that ʿAmr ibn Maymūn Al-Awdī said: "Once, Muʿādh ibn Jabal stood up among us and said, 'O Children of Awd! I am the emissary of Allah's Messenger ﷺ to you; know that the Return is to Allah, either to Paradise or the Fire.'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah the same way: ultimately everyone returns to Allah on the Day of Resurrection and gives an account of his actions.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a second, complementary sense from some commentators: human thought and imagination itself comes to its end at Allah. The reality of His Being and His Attributes cannot be discovered by human imagination, because it lies beyond conceptualisation — so we are prohibited from probing into them in that way. The narrations, it says, direct us to ponder the manifestations of His attributes and His bounties, and not to try to conceptualise His Being or the reality of His Attributes, which is left to His knowledge alone. That is the believer's way: affirm in full what He has told us of Himself, and stop where knowledge stops.

## Living it

- **Watch for your own *kudyah*.** Every serious act of obedience eventually hits rock — the giving that begins to pinch, the habit that stops being exciting. Ayah 34 names the moment a man says "we are finished" and walks away from a half-dug well.
- **Miserliness is a theory about the future you cannot possibly hold.** Ayah 35 asks where you got your data; 34:39 answers the fear — whatever you spend, He replaces it.
- **Stop shopping for someone to carry it.** No friend, no lineage, no witnessed document transfers a single sin. Ayah 38 closes that market permanently.
- **Nobody can pray your prayer for you — so pray it.** For what *is* transferable, keep giving: duʿāʼ, charity, and reward conveyed to others as the scholars have described.
- **Plant traces.** A righteous child, an ongoing charity, knowledge people benefit from — these keep striving for you when you no longer can.
- **Mind the intention now.** Ayah 40 says the striving will be *seen*; ayah 41 that it will be paid in full; ayah 42 that the road ends at your Lord.

passages.title: He alone makes laugh, weep, live, die
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

These ayat are a chain of statements about what Allah does. Ibn Kathir heads the whole section: "Some Attributes of the Lord, that He returns Man as He originated Him, and some of what He does with His Servants."

Read them the way Ibn Kathir sets them out, one after another:

> And that it is He Who makes laugh, and makes weep (43) And that it is He Who causes death and gives life (44) And that He creates the pairs, male and female (45) From Nutfah when it is emitted (46) And that upon Him is another bringing forth (Resurrection) (47) And that it is He Who Aghna and Aqna (48) And that He is the Lord of Ash-Shi'ra (49)

Notice the shape of it. Each statement is introduced the same way — "and that… and that… and that…" — so they arrive as a series of facts laid one beside the other, each carrying the same weight. Notice too that ayah 46 is not a fresh item on the list: Ibn Kathir quotes 45 and 46 together as a single sentence — "(And that He creates the pairs, male and female. From Nutfah when it is emitted.)" The drop belongs to the statement about the pairs.

**The clause they all hang from.** The chain is still governed by ayah 42 immediately before it: *"And that to your Lord is the End."* Ibn Kathir explains this as "the return of everything on the Day of Resurrection." He then cites what Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from 'Amr bin Maymun Al-Awdi: Mu'adh bin Jabal once stood up among his people and said, "O Children of Awd! I am the emissary of Allah's Messenger ﷺ to you; know that the Return is to Allah, either to Paradise or the Fire."

So read 43–49 with that as the frame. This is not a nature-appreciation list. It is the same Lord who holds your laughter, your tears, your birth, your death, your wealth and the star over your head — and who is also the destination of everything.

---

## A note on how these ayat are worded

Something in these sentences resists a flat English rendering, and you can see it in how carefully the sources themselves translate.

Ibn Kathir does not render ayah 43 as "He makes laugh." He renders it *"it is **He** Who makes you laugh, and makes you weep"* — and the same emphatic shape for 44, 48 and 49: "it is He Who causes death and gives life," "it is He Who Aghna and Aqna," "He is the Lord of Ash-Shi'ra." The translation of ayah 49 given with our text goes further still: *"And He **alone** is the Lord of Sirius."* The emphasis is not decoration added by translators struggling for effect; it is what the sentences are doing.

And look at what the human being is in these sentences. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders ayah 43 as "He is the One who makes **[one]** laugh and makes **[him]** weep" — the brackets are the translator supplying the missing person, because the person is the one being *acted upon*. We are the object in these verses, not the subject.

---

## Ayah 43 — laughter and tears

*"Moreover, He is the One Who brings about joy and sadness."*

Ibn Kathir's explanation is precise and worth reading slowly. It means "that He created in His creatures the ability to laugh or weep **and the causes for each of these opposites**."

Two separate creations are being affirmed there — the *capacity* placed inside us, and the *occasions* that set it off. The joy and the news that brought the joy are both from Him. The grief and the loss that caused the grief are both from Him.

**Why this ayah is harder than it looks.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts its finger on exactly the place where we go wrong. Mankind experiences happiness and grief, and so laughs and weeps — but man "assigns this to the secondary causes," to the existent things of this universe, "and that is where he ends the matter." We trace the tears back to the phone call, the diagnosis, the person who wronged us, and we stop there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that if we analyse carefully and profoundly, the whole system of cause and effect ends with Allah, the Primary and Supreme Cause. No secondary cause makes anyone happy or sad, nor makes him laugh or weep. Both of these things are created by Allah. He is the One who created the series of secondary causes and effects in our finite world in the first place — and as the Primary and Supreme Cause, "He can at any moment make the laughing person weep, and make the weeping person laugh."

Note carefully what this does and does not say. It does not deny that causes exist — it says Allah created the chain of them. This is the balance the passage strikes: take your medicine, thank the friend, but do not let the chain terminate anywhere short of Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the point by quoting a couplet, which asks Allah what He whispered into the ear of the flower that it is smiling, and what He said to the nightingale that it is weeping all the time. The smile and the lament in creation both have the same Author.

---

## Ayah 44 — death and life

*"And He is the One Who gives life and causes death."*

Ibn Kathir supports this ayah with a parallel verse: *"Who has created death and life"* (67:2).

That parallel is doing real work. Death is not simply an absence, an accident that interrupts life. It is spoken of as something **created** — deliberately made, placed in the design like everything else. The verse Ibn Kathir reaches for puts death and life side by side as two things brought into being by the same Maker.

Placed immediately after the laughing and weeping of ayah 43, the movement of the list is worth pausing over: the smallest fluctuations of your inner state and the largest facts of your existence are named in consecutive breaths, and both are traced to the same hand.

---

## Ayat 45–47 — from a drop to a second creation

*"And He created the pairs — males and females — from a sperm-drop when it is emitted. And it is upon Him to bring about re-creation."*

Here the list stops being merely a list and becomes an **argument**. Ibn Kathir quotes 45 and 46 as one sentence and then reinforces them with a passage from Surah al-Qiyamah, which he gives in full:

> *"Does man think that he will be left neglected? Was he not a Nutfah? Then he became an 'Alaqah (something that clings); then Allah shaped and fashioned him in due proportion. And made of him two sexes, male and female. Is not He able to give life to the dead?"* (75:36–40)

Follow the steps as Ibn Kathir has arranged them:

- **The starting material is nothing to boast of.** A *nuṭfah* is a drop of fluid, "when it is emitted." That is the raw material of every human being who has ever made a claim about himself.
- **Yet out of that drop comes differentiation.** The same fluid yields *az-zawjayn*, the pair — male and female. Ibn Kathir's supporting verse follows the identical sequence: a drop, then something that clings, then shaping and fashioning, then "two sexes, male and female."
- **Therefore the question at the end answers itself.** The passage he quotes closes by turning on the reader: *"Is not He able to give life to the dead?"*

**Ayah 47 and its wording.** This ayah does not say "and that He is able to bring about the second creation." Its wording is *wa-anna **'alayhi** an-nash'ata al-ukhrā* — "and that **upon Him** is another bringing forth." Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: "just as He first originated creation, He is able to bring it back to life, resurrecting it for the Day of Judgement."

That is the whole argument of these three ayat compressed into one line. The One who did it from a drop is the One who will do it again.

---

## Ayah 48 — *aghnā wa aqnā*

*"And He is the One Who enriches and impoverishes."*

This is the one ayah in the passage where the commentators genuinely differ, and the honest thing is to lay the readings side by side rather than flatten them into one.

- **Ibn Kathir's own summary.** He glosses the two words as "Aghna (gives much) and Aqna (a little)," and then explains: it is Allah Who gives wealth to His servants and this wealth *remains* with them — meaning they are able to use it to their benefit — and this is out of the completeness of His favour. He notes that most of the statements of the scholars of tafsir revolve around this meaning, citing Abu Salih, Ibn Jarir and others.
- **Mujahid:** *aghnā* means He gives wealth; *aqnā* means He gives servants. Qatadah said similarly.
- **Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid:** *aghnā* means He granted; *aqnā* means He gave contentment.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, on the roots:** *ghinā* means affluence, and *ighnā'* means to give wealth to somebody else and enrich him. *Aqnā* is derived from *qinyah*, which means preserving and reserving wealth. So the meaning is that Allah enriches His servants and grants them wealth to their satisfaction, so that they are able to use some and keep some in reserve for future use.

Two things follow.

First, on every one of these readings the ayah is about **Allah's giving**. The wealth, the ability to keep it, the ability to benefit from it, and even the contentment that makes wealth feel like wealth — all of it is named as His gift, not as a return on our cleverness.

Second, you will meet the two verbs rendered as opposites — "enriches and impoverishes" — as in the translation printed with this ayah. The commentators quoted above do not read them that way. They take *aqnā* as a *further favour*: property that stays, servants, reserve, contentment. If you meet both renderings, this is the reason for the difference.

---

## Ayah 49 — Lord of Ash-Shi'rā

*"And He alone is the Lord of Sirius."*

Of all the stars in the sky, why name this one? Because of who was listening.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word: *shi'rā*, with the diacritical mark *kasrah* — the short "i" vowel — under the letter *shīn*, is the name of a star, called Sirius, which is behind Jauzā'. Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd all said about *Ash-Shi'rā* that it is the bright star named *Mirzam Al-Jawzā'* (Sirius), **which a group of Arabs used to worship**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail that makes sense of the practice: some of the Arab tribes worshipped this mighty star because they regarded it as a source of good or bad luck for them.

So this ayah is aimed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit about why: Allah mentions this star in particular in order to refute their false notion and to affirm that He is the Lord and Master of *this star as well* — although He is the Creator, Master and Lord of all the stars, the heavens and the earth.

The object of their devotion is demoted in a single word: *Rabb ash-Shi'rā*. What they worshipped has a Lord.

---

## Living it

**Do not stop at the second cause.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is meant to change how you narrate your own day. When something delights you, the chain of thanks does not end with the person who arranged it. When something breaks you, the chain of complaint does not end with whoever caused it. Trace both back to the One who created the capacity and the occasion alike.

**Hold your state loosely.** If He "can at any moment make the laughing person weep, and make the weeping person laugh," then neither your present ease nor your present grief is the settled truth about you. That is a warning against arrogance in comfort and a mercy against despair in hardship — from the same sentence.

**Read your own origin honestly.** Ayah 46 says you began as a drop. Ibn Kathir uses that fact twice over: to place the human being's true starting point in front of him, and to answer the question of whether being raised again is beyond Allah — *"Is not He able to give life to the dead?"*

**Let wealth be received, not credited to yourself.** On every reading of ayah 48 — wealth, servants, reserve, contentment — what is described is something given. A person who understands that does not become proud in abundance nor bitter in less.

**Check what you have made a Shi'rā of.** A bright thing was worshipped because people believed it dictated their fortune, good or bad. Ayah 49 does not deny the star exists or that it is impressive; it puts a Lord over it. Whatever you quietly believe controls your luck — an income, an institution, a person, a plan — has a Lord over it too.

passages.title: The nations He destroyed - which favour will you dispute?
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close a long chain of statements about what Allah alone does — and they close it with history. Having said that He is the One who makes people laugh and weep, who gives death and life, who grants and gives contentment, the passage now points to four vanished nations and asks the listener a single question: after all this, **which favour of your Lord will you dispute?**

## One long sentence, and where it comes from

Ayat 50 to 54 are not free-standing announcements. They continue a chain of clauses that began earlier in the sūrah, each one opening the same way — "and that He…", "and that He…" — running through ayah 42 ("and that to your Lord is the End"), ayah 44 ("and that it is He who causes death and gives life"), ayah 47 ("and that upon Him is another bringing forth"), ayah 49 ("and that He is the Lord of Ash-Shiʿrā"), and then arriving at ayah 50: "and that it is He who destroyed the former ʿĀd."

This matters because of what that chain is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes at the end of ayah 54: **"Here ends the teachings of the scriptures of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm."** In other words, the whole run — the attributes, the creation of male and female from a drop, the resurrection, and now the destroyed nations — is being presented as the content of the earlier revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point at ayah 55, describing the signs in the scriptures of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm that support and substantiate the claims of the Prophet ﷺ about the truth of his revelation. The deniers are not being told something newly invented. They are being told what scripture before them already said.

So the destroyed nations arrive in this passage not as a change of subject but as part of the same argument. He who makes you laugh and weep, who grants and gives contentment — He is also the One who ended ʿĀd, Thamūd, Nūh's people and Lūt's cities. The Lord of your private fortunes is the Lord of the graveyards of nations.

## Ayah 50: "the former ʿĀd"

Ibn Kathir identifies them precisely: ʿĀd al-ūlā are **the people of Hūd**, descendants of ʿĀd, son of Iram, son of Sām, son of Nūh. He connects them to Allah's words elsewhere: "Saw you not how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd — of Iram, with the lofty pillars, the like of which were not created in the land?" (89:6-8).

Note that description. *The like of which were not created in the land.* Ibn Kathir says plainly that the people of ʿĀd were **among the strongest, fiercest people and the most rebellious against Allah and His Messenger** — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān repeats the same description word for word. This is not a story about a weak nation being crushed.

**Why "the former" (al-ūlā)?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that there are two branches of this people, one called *ūlā* (the first, the earlier) and one *ukhrā* (the latter, the second). The ayah specifies the first. Maʿārif adds, on the authority of Mazharī, that ʿĀd were **the first nation destroyed by punishment after the destruction of the people of Nūh** (peace be upon him).

**How they were destroyed:** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Hūd (peace be upon him) was sent to them and they disobeyed him, and as a result Allah annihilated the entire nation by a violently furious wind. Ibn Kathir cites the verse describing it: "By a furious violent wind! Which Allah imposed on them for seven nights and eight days in succession" (69:6-7). The strongest of peoples, undone by moving air — for seven nights and eight days in succession.

## Ayah 51: "and Thamūd — He spared none"

*Wa Thamūda fa-mā abqā.* Ibn Kathir's gloss on **fa-mā abqā** is stark: it "declares that He destroyed them all and spared none of them." The Arabic is short and final — *He did not leave over.* Not a defeat, not a decimation. A closed account.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the history: Sālih (peace be upon him) was sent to the tribe of Thamūd, whom it describes as "the second ʿĀd," and they too disobeyed their Prophet. Those who transgressed **were caught by the awesome Cry of Jibrāʼīl (peace be upon him), and their hearts were burst by the horrific sound**, resulting in the mass destruction of those people.

*A reflection on these two together:* set the punishments side by side and something becomes visible. ʿĀd were destroyed by a wind; Thamūd by a sound. Neither of these is an army; neither is a rival civilisation. Whatever such a people could fortify themselves against, it was not this.

## Ayah 52: the people of Nūh

"And the people of Nūh aforetime" — Ibn Kathir clarifies the timing simply: **before ʿĀd and Thamūd**. The passage has just named ʿĀd and Thamūd, and now reaches back past both.

Then the ayah adds a judgement: **"Verily, they were more unjust and more rebellious and transgressing."** Ibn Kathir explains: **more unjust in disobeying Allah than those who came after them.**

This is worth pausing over. The passage does not flatten all disbelief into one undifferentiated mass. It grades it. Some nations went further than others, and the ayah states the comparison plainly: the people of Nūh outdid those who came after them in *zulm* (wrongdoing) and *tughyān* (overstepping every limit).

## Ayat 53-54: the overturned cities

**"And He destroyed the overthrown cities"** — *wal-muʼtafikata ahwā*. Ibn Kathir explains that this means the cities (Sodom and Gomorrah) to which the Prophet Lūt was sent, and that **Allah turned their cities upside down over them and sent on them stones of Sijjīl**.

On the word itself, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *muʼtafikah* literally means *muʼtalifah*, "joined together," and that these were a few settlements adjacent to the city; Lūt (peace be upon him) was sent to them, and **because of disobedience and commission of shameful and unspeakable sins, their cities were turned upside down by Jibrāʼīl** (peace be upon him). So the plural is not loose speech: it was a cluster of linked settlements, and the whole cluster went together.

The translation renders *ahwā* as "He turned the cities"; Ibn Kathir's gloss is that Allah turned them upside down over their own inhabitants. Whatever a person had built, the roof of it became the thing that fell on him.

Then ayah 54: **"How overwhelming was what covered them!"** — *fa-ghashshāhā mā ghashshā*. Ibn Kathir renders the construction as "whatever has covered it, has covered it," and connects it to the stones of Sijjīl that Allah sent on them, quoting: "And We rained on them a rain (of torment). And how evil was the rain of those who had been warned!" (26:173).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit about the order: **the cities were first overturned, and after that stones of hard clay were sent down on them, which covered them.** Overturned, then buried. The site was not merely destroyed; it was covered over.

And note the phrase Ibn Kathir cites: *those who had been warned*. In these four cases the commentaries name the messenger each time: Hūd sent to ʿĀd, Sālih sent to Thamūd, Lūt sent to the overturned cities — and the fourth nation is identified in the Qur'an itself by the name of its Prophet, the people of Nūh. That fact is about to become the whole point.

## Ayah 55: "which of your Lord's favours will you dispute?"

*Fa-bi-ayyi ālāʼi rabbika tatamārā.*

**The verb.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it directly: **tamārā means to dispute and oppose.** Ibn Kathir's rendering is "doubt," while the sense Maʿārif brings out is argumentative — the posture of someone opposing rather than someone still weighing.

**Who is being addressed?** The commentators record two views, and Ibn Kathir reports both:

- **Qatādah** understood it as addressed to the human being in general: "which of Allah's favours for you, O man, do you doubt?"
- **Ibn Jurayj** held that it is directed towards the Prophet ﷺ — "O Muhammad!"

Ibn Kathir judges the first explanation better, and notes that this is the meaning **Ibn Jarīr preferred**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same position from **Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him): the verse is addressed to every human being.** So the weight of the commentary places you, the reader, in the vocative. The finger points outward from the page.

**Why call these things "favours"?** *Ālāʼ* means graces, bounties, favours — and the passage has just finished describing four annihilations. How is that a bounty?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers this beautifully. After so many clear and invincible arguments in the preceding verses, and the signs in the scriptures of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm that support and substantiate the claims of the Prophet ﷺ about the truth of his revelation, the verse says to the obstinate disbelievers: *how long will you continue to deny the truth and wander in the wilderness of disbelief?* It makes abundantly clear, for those who think and deliberate, that there should be no room for any doubt in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his revelation and his teachings. And then it makes the crucial point — **having heard about the stories of destruction and punishment of past nations, this is an opportune occasion for them to straighten out. This well-timed occasion is a favour of Allah. They should take advantage of it instead of fighting and opposing it.**

That is the hinge of the whole passage, in Maʿārif's reading. The ruins themselves are the mercy: you are hearing the record of what happened, and the hearing of it in time is the favour. Disputing that is disputing the very opportunity being handed to you.

## What the passage asks of us

*The following are reflections drawn from the commentary above, not further statements of the commentators.*

**Read the ruins as an argument, not as folklore.** Ibn Kathir presents ʿĀd not as legend but as lineage — descendants of ʿĀd, son of Iram, son of Sām, son of Nūh — and their fate as documented event. When you pass what remains of a once-great power, this passage wants that to register as information about how the world is actually run.

**Do not measure your safety by your strength.** The sharpest detail here is that both commentaries call ʿĀd "among the strongest, fiercest people" — and both then report, in the same breath, that Allah annihilated the entire nation. Whatever you are relying on to feel secure — resources, status, competence — a people described in those terms had more of it.

**Take the warning while it is still a warning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of ayah 55 turns the passage from a threat into an opportunity with a closing date: the well-timed occasion is itself a favour, and the response is what is being asked for.

**Let the question land on you.** Both Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) read ayah 55 as addressed to every human being. So read it in the second person, and answer it honestly: of everything Allah has given — the laughter, the tears, the life, the provision, the contentment, the warning that came in time — *which one of them are you prepared to argue with?*

These are the closing verses of Sūrat an-Najm — the words on which the whole sūrah lands. Allah turns and speaks directly to the listener: the one standing before you is a warner of the same kind as the warners of old, the Hour he warns of has drawn near — and you are laughing. The passage moves in one unbroken line from *who he is* (56), to *what is coming* (57–58), to *how you are receiving it* (59–61), and finally to the one response that fits: **fall down in prostration** (62). It ends not with an argument but with a body on the ground.

## "This is a warner from the warners of old" (56)

The verse opens with a demonstrative — *hādhā*, "this". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that it may point to the Holy Prophet ﷺ himself or to the Qur'an he has brought. Read of the Prophet ﷺ, the meaning is that in the past many Prophets were sent to their respective nations, and he is sent to all mankind; he is not a new thing among the Messengers, and he is well-established in the straight path. Read of the Qur'an, the meaning is that he has come with a book of guidance which, if complied with, assures success in this world and in the Hereafter — and the opponents should fear the Divine punishment.

Ibn Kathir takes *hādhā* as referring to Muhammad ﷺ, and reads *min an-nudhur al-ūlā* — "from the warners of old" — as: just like the warners of old, he was sent as a Messenger as they were sent as Messengers. He brings the parallel verse, **"Say: I am not a new thing among the Messengers"** (46:9).

That is a quietly disarming answer to any charge of novelty. The verse does not defend him as unprecedented; it places him in a line. Whatever is strange about him is not that he is new, but that he is the latest in a long succession of men sent to say the same thing — and both commentaries make the same point in different words: he is not a new thing among the Messengers.

## Al-Āzifah: the thing that is almost here (57–58)

Ayah 57 is two words in Arabic and almost impossible to render fully: *azifat al-āzifah*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verb *azifa* is used in the sense of *qaruba*, which means to draw near, and that *āzifah* is the feminine active participle from that same verb, referring to the Imminent Event. Literally, then: **"The Approaching One has approached."** The name of the thing and the verb of the thing are the same root, doubled back on itself. The Day of Resurrection is not merely described as near; nearness is its very name, and now that nearness is announced as having arrived.

Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: that which is near — the Day of Resurrection — has drawn nearer. And he links it to the opening of the very next sūrah, **"The Hour has drawn near"** (54:1).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the perspective that makes this intelligible to anyone tempted to object that centuries have passed: the imminence of the Resurrection is stated **in relation to the age of the entire world**, and the ummah of the Holy Prophet ﷺ is right at the end of it, near the Day of Judgment. Nearness here is measured against the whole sweep of history, not against a human lifetime.

Then ayah 58: *laysa lahā min dūni'llāhi kāshifah* — rendered here "None but Allah can disclose it." The commentators read *kāshifah* in the sense of removing or averting: Ibn Kathir says no one besides Allah can prevent it from coming, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise says no one besides Allah can prevent it from happening. Both then add the second half of the point — **nor does anyone know when it will come, except Him**. Both doors are shut at once. No one can push the Hour back, and no one can find out its date. All that is left to a human being is to be ready.

## "I am the naked warner"

Why is the tone of this passage so urgent? Ibn Kathir puts it in a sentence: the warner is eager to convey his knowledge of the imminence of a calamity, so that it does not befall those to whom he is a warner. He cites **"He is only a warner to you in face of a severe torment"** (34:46), and then a ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ said: **"I am the naked warner."** (The commentary quotes this without naming the collection it comes from.)

Ibn Kathir explains the image: *I was in such a hurry to warn against the evil I saw coming that I did not wear anything* — one rushes to warn his people in such haste that he will be naked. He arrives stripped, and the very fact that he did not pause to dress is itself the message: *there is no time*. Ibn Kathir says explicitly that this meaning befits the meaning of the ayah *azifat al-āzifah*. A warner has come; the thing he warns of is at the door.

## Why the small things matter

Ibn Kathir places a ḥadīth here that at first seems to change the subject, and then does not. Imam Ahmad recorded that Sahl bin Saʿd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Beware of small sins! The example of the effect of small sin is that of people who settled near the bottom of a valley. One of them brought a piece of wood, and another brought another piece of wood, until they cooked their bread! Verily, small sins will destroy its companion, if one is held accountable for them."

Nobody in that valley carried a log. Each person carried one piece of wood — a nothing, a triviality — and between them they built a fire hot enough to bake with. That is how a life is lost: not by one catastrophic act, but by the accumulation of things too small to notice. Placed beside *azifat al-āzifah*, the ḥadīth lands with force: the fire is being assembled twig by twig, and the Day of accounting is not distant.

## Laughter where tears belong (59–61)

Ayah 59 opens with a question that is really an indictment: *a-fa-min hādha'l-ḥadīthi taʿjabūn* — "Do you then wonder at this discourse?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies "this discourse" as the Qur'an: the Divine Discourse, which is itself a miracle, has already come to them — and they are surprised at it, and laugh in jest and mock at it, and do not weep at their sins and shortcomings.

Ibn Kathir reads the three verbs as a sequence of a single attitude. **"You wonder"** — doubting that it is true. **"And you laugh"** — in jest and mock at it. **"And weep not"** — just as those who believe in it weep, of whom Allah says, **"And they fall down on their faces weeping and it increases their humility"** (17:109). Notice how exactly that verse mirrors the end of our passage: falling down, weeping, humility — the believers already do what ayah 62 is about to command.

Then ayah 61: *wa antum sāmidūn*. The commentators give this word two readings, and both are worth holding:

- **Heedlessness.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *sāmidūn* is the plural of *sāmid*, from the root *sumūd*, which literally denotes to be heedless, and is used in the sense of *ghāfilūn* — unmindful. Ibn Kathir reports a narration from Ibn ʿAbbās that *sāmidūn* means "turning away", and says similar was reported from Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah.
- **Singing.** Ibn Kathir reports, through Sufyān ath-Thawrī from his father, that Ibn ʿAbbās said *sāmidūn* means "singing", and that in the Yemenite dialect *ismid for us* means "sing for us"; ʿIkrimah said something similar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some of the Imams have interpreted *sumūd* to mean to sing, and that this meaning can equally fit or apply in this context.

Both readings describe one scene. The Qur'an is being recited — the most serious speech in existence, announcing an Event nobody can avert — and the audience is amusing itself. Ibn Kathir sums up the whole reproach in a phrase: they hear the Qur'an, **yet they turn away from it in heedless play**. Whether they drown out the recitation with song or simply turn their faces away, the failing is the same: treating an emergency as entertainment.

There is a diagnosis buried in ayah 60 worth sitting with. Allah does not merely condemn the laughter; He names the missing tears — *"and you laugh and weep not."* Laughter at revelation is bad; the absence of weeping is what exposes the heart. A person who could hear that the Hour is at hand and feel nothing has not made an intellectual error; something in him has gone numb.

## "So fall down in prostration to Allah, and worship Him" (62)

The passage does not end by winning the argument. It ends with a command to the body.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion plainly: the preceding verses hold a lesson for everyone who considers them seriously — that he should worship Allah and bow down before Him in humbleness. Ibn Kathir says that Allah here ordered His servants to prostrate to Him, to worship Him according to the way of His Messenger ﷺ, and to fulfil the requirement of *tawḥīd* (Allah's absolute oneness, including His exclusive right to be worshipped) and sincerity. His gloss on the verse is: **with submission, sincerity, and tawḥīd**.

Two conditions are packed into two words. *Fasjudū li'llāh* — prostrate **to Allah**: that is tawḥīd and sincerity. *Waʿbudū* — and worship, in the manner the Messenger ﷺ taught: that is how it is to be done. Sajdah is the exact opposite of everything in ayahs 59–61. Mockery looks down on something; prostration puts one's own face on the floor. Heedless play is the body at leisure; sajdah is the body stopped.

The verse carries the prostration mark (۩) in the muṣḥaf, and the reports that follow — of the Prophet ﷺ prostrating on reciting the sūrah, and of the discussion over whether that prostration is obligatory — all turn on that.

## The day the whole assembly went down

This is where the passage becomes a scene, and both commentaries preserve it.

Al-Bukhari recorded, through Abu Maʿmar from ʿAbdul-Warith from Ayyūb from ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Prophet ﷺ prostrated upon reciting An-Najm and the Muslims, idolators, Jinns and mankind who were present prostrated along with him." (Ibn Kathir's text adds: "Only Muslim collected this Hadith.") Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same report from Ibn ʿAbbās on the authority of Bukhari. Picture it: the sūrah has just announced the Hour as imminent, exposed the laughter of the mockers, and closed with a command — and everyone present, believer and idolater alike, went down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the report of ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd, recorded in Bukhari and Muslim: when the Holy Prophet ﷺ finished reciting the sūrah before a mixed gathering of Muslims and disbelievers and prostrated along with his followers, the disbelievers prostrated too — **except one old Quraishi man, who took a handful of soil, applied it to his forehead, and said, "This is enough for me."** Ibn Masʿūd said he saw this man later on killed as a disbeliever.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers this reading of what happened: following the example of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, the Muslims were expected to prostrate; as for the idolaters, having been profoundly impressed with the solemnity of the occasion and being overawed by the august recitation of the Qur'anic words, as well as by the Divine Majesty and Glory, they might also have fallen in prostration. Because that prostration was performed in a state of disbelief it carried no reward — but it did leave a deep impression on them, and as a result of that impact they all later embraced the Islamic faith, except the one person who died in the state of *kufr*, because he arrogantly refrained from performing the sajdah.

That single handful of soil is the whole passage in miniature. He was moved — he did something with his hands, he could not simply sit still — but he would not put his face on the ground. Pride will negotiate almost anything except surrender.

Ibn Kathir preserves a first-person memory of the same kind. Imam Ahmad recorded that Al-Muṭṭalib bin Abī Wadāʿah said: "While in Makkah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once recited Surat An-Najm, then prostrated along with all those who were with him at the time. I raised my head, however, and I refused to prostrate." Al-Muṭṭalib had not embraced Islam yet — but ever since he became Muslim, he would never hear anyone recite this sūrah until the end without prostrating with whomever was prostrating after reciting it. Ibn Kathir adds that An-Nasa'i also collected this ḥadīth, in the Book of Al-Bukhari, excluding prayer, in his Sunan. The man who once lifted his head spent the rest of his life lowering it, every time those words were recited.

## A note on the ruling

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises an apparent difficulty and answers it. The Ṣaḥīḥain record a report from Zayd Ibn Thābit that he recited the entire Sūrah An-Najm in the presence of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, but the Prophet ﷺ did not perform the sajdah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that it does not necessarily follow from this that the sajdah is not obligatory or compulsory: it is possible that at that particular moment he did not have his ablution, or that there was some other legitimate reason for not performing it. In such situations, it argues, it is not obligatory to perform the sajdah forthwith; it can be delayed until the reason has ceased — and Allah, the Pure and Exalted, knows best.

## Living it

The passage closes the sūrah by handing the reader a single action, and it is worth taking literally.

**Do not let the recitation pass as noise.** The reproach in ayahs 59–61 is aimed, in Ibn Kathir's words, at people who *hear* the Qur'an yet turn away from it in heedless play. Half-listening while entertained is nearer to *sāmidūn* than most of us would like.

**Watch for the missing tears.** Ayah 60 measures the heart by what is absent. If words about the Hour produce nothing at all, that is information — and Ibn Kathir's answer to it is the believers of 17:109, who fall down on their faces weeping and are only increased in humility.

**Take the small sins seriously.** The ḥadīth of Sahl bin Saʿd says it is the pieces of wood nobody counted that cooked the bread. The person who tells himself there is time is exactly the person ayah 57 is addressing.

**And then prostrate.** Ibn Kathir's three words — submission, sincerity, tawḥīd — are the whole of the response: to Allah, in the way the Messenger ﷺ taught. That is how Sūrat an-Najm ends, and it is how a life that has understood it ends too.
